title: System Design: 4 Cycles to Senior-Level Fluency
how_it_works: Static data, no AI at runtime. 16 sessions in 4 weekly cycles. Each cycle is Monday, Wednesday, Friday (learn) then Sunday morning (mock). Each session has day_offset = days after start_date, and start_date must be a Monday. The Watch card shows the session whose date is today; on off days it shows the next upcoming session plus any missed ones with a catch-up badge. Mark done stores one completion row per session. A learn session is: 5-minute warm-up recall, 35 to 45 minutes of reading, then say-it-out-loud lines, interviewer follow-ups, and drills. A mock session is: 5-minute warm-up, a 45-minute voice mock with an AI interviewer, then logging the transcript and scores in the System Design note tab.

cycles.theme: Foundations: numbers, the request path, and choosing storage
Distribution: partitioning, replication, async systems, and consistency
Depth: storage engines, transactions, and reliability engineering
Senior judgment: specialized components, production reality, communication, capstone

rubric: Requirements: asks scoping questions in order and declares assumptions out loud
Estimation: correct units, correct order of magnitude, and a 'so what' that drives the architecture
Components and vocabulary: uses the standard industry names correctly (WebSocket vs webhook, consistent hashing, etc.)
Ownership: declares constraints and makes decisions instead of deferring
Trade-offs: states the cost of each choice, the rejected alternative, and what would change the choice
Pacing and depth: finishes all phases in 45 minutes and goes deep on the hardest part
level_calibration: Score each category 1 to 5. Anchor: 1 = misses it entirely. 2 = new-grad baseline, names components but little justification. 3 = solid mid-level, justified choices, some numbers. 4 = senior habits, quantified, anticipates failure, owns trade-offs. 5 = staff-level, drives the conversation, simplifies the problem, and teaches the interviewer something. A strong new-grad target is 3 across the board with 4 in estimation and trade-offs.
baseline_note: Before session 1, save your baseline AI review in the System Design note tab titled 'AI review: baseline'. The final review in session 16 is compared against it.
mock_prompt_template: Act as a system design interviewer at a large tech company, calibrated for a strong new-grad candidate being evaluated against senior-level habits. Today's prompt: [PASTE PROMPT]. Rules: (1) Do not teach or give hints during the interview. (2) If I say 'it depends' or defer, push back and make me decide and justify. (3) Let me ask scoping questions first and answer them briefly. (4) Keep a running clock and warn me if any phase runs more than 3 minutes long. (5) Check my math: if I'm off by 10x or more, interrupt and make me recompute. (6) During the deep dive, ask at least 4 pressure questions of the form 'what breaks first', 'what happens if X fails', 'how does this change at 10x', and 'why not Y'. (7) At about 40 minutes, stop and score me 1 to 5 on each of: requirements, estimation, components and vocabulary, ownership, trade-offs, pacing and depth. For every score, quote a specific thing I said. Then list the exact terms I got wrong or missed, the biggest single mistake, and the one habit to fix before the next mock. Do not be generous.
final_review_prompt: Below are my System Design entries: my baseline review, four mock transcripts with their AI scores, and my own notes on what I got wrong. Using the six categories (requirements, estimation, components and vocabulary, ownership, trade-offs, pacing and depth), score my current level 1 to 5 on each, with a one-line justification quoting my own words. Compare each category to my baseline and show the trend across the four mocks. Be critical, not generous. List the top 3 weaknesses still holding me back, the specific terms I still miss, and whether the habits I showed are closer to new-grad, mid-level, or senior. End with a 7-day plan of exactly what to practice next. Do not give general advice, only things supported by the entries.

sessions.title: The estimation machine: units, time, latency, and server counts
sessions.goal: Make estimation a reflex: correct units, correct order of magnitude, and a clear 'so what' that drives an architecture decision.
sessions.warmup_note: Cold start. Answer these out loud BEFORE reading anything, then check. Write your score in the note tab so you can see improvement by session 16.

warmup.q: 12 billion records x 500 bytes. How many TB?
2 billion writes per day. Average writes per second, and the number you design for?
warmup.a: About 23,000 per second average (2 x 10^9 / 86,400). Design for peak, about 2x to 3x, so roughly 50,000 to 70,000.

warmup.q: Roughly how much faster is reading from memory than a random read from an SSD?
warmup.a: About 1,000x (about 100 ns vs about 100 microseconds).

sections.heading: Why estimation is a senior skill
sections.body: In a design interview, estimation is not a math test. It is how you earn the right to make architecture decisions. A senior engineer says 'that's about 40,000 writes per second, which is too much for one node, so I'm partitioning' and the number carries the argument. A weaker candidate says 'we should probably shard' with nothing behind it. Your baseline review showed your reasoning was right and the units slipped: 6 trillion bytes became 6,000 TB. That error is fixable with a routine, not talent. The routine is: convert to scientific notation, multiply the coefficients, add the exponents, then read the unit off the exponent.

sections.heading: The unit ladder and the zero-count
sections.body: Use powers of 1,000 in interviews. 1 KB = 10^3 bytes, 1 MB = 10^6, 1 GB = 10^9, 1 TB = 10^12, 1 PB = 10^15, 1 EB = 10^18. Each rung is three zeros. To convert any byte count, write it as a x 10^n, then divide n by 3 and take the remainder as leftover zeros. 6 x 10^12 has n = 12, so 12/3 = 4 rungs above bytes (KB, MB, GB, TB) and the unit is TB with no leftover. 6 x 10^13 is 60 TB. 6 x 10^15 is 6 PB. When you finish a calculation, say the unit out loud and ask yourself whether it sounds plausible: 'six thousand terabytes for 12 billion small records? No, that's off by a thousand.' That 3-second sanity check would have caught your slip.

sections.heading: Time constants, QPS, and the two shortcuts
sections.body: A day has 86,400 seconds, which you round to 10^5 for speed. A month is about 2.5 million seconds and a year about 31.5 million (3 x 10^7). Shortcut one: QPS is daily volume divided by 10^5, so 1 million events a day is about 12 per second, and 1 billion a day is about 12,000 per second. Shortcut two: peak is 2x to 3x the average for steady consumer traffic, and can be 10x or more for spiky traffic (flash sales, live events, campaigns). Always say which you are using: 'Average is about 12,000 per second. I'll design for about 35,000 at peak.' Interviewers listen for the word 'peak' because systems break at peak, not at average.

sections.heading: Bits vs bytes and bandwidth
sections.body: Storage is quoted in bytes, networks in bits. 1 byte = 8 bits. A 1 Gbps link moves at most 125 MB per second, and a 10 Gbps link about 1.25 GB per second. When you compute bandwidth, multiply bytes per second by 8 to get bits per second. Example: 100,000 requests per second at 20 KB each is 2 GB per second, which is 16 Gbps. That already exceeds one 10 Gbps network card, so you need multiple machines or a CDN, and it also tells you bandwidth cost will matter. Egress (data leaving a cloud provider) is usually one of the most expensive line items, which is why media-heavy designs lean on CDNs.

sections.heading: Latency numbers: remember the ratios
sections.body: Approximate figures: a main-memory read about 100 ns. A random SSD read about 100 microseconds (fast NVMe can be tens of microseconds). A round trip inside one data center about 0.5 ms. A spinning-disk seek about 10 ms. A round trip within a continent tens of milliseconds, and across an ocean roughly 100 to 200 ms. These shift as hardware improves, so memorize the ratios: memory is about 1,000x faster than SSD, SSD is about 100x faster than a disk seek, and a trans-oceanic hop costs about as much as a million memory reads. Consequences you can state in an interview: put the hot working set in memory, avoid synchronous cross-region calls on the request path, prefer sequential over random IO, and batch small operations so you pay the round trip once. Also remember latency adds up serially: 20 sequential database calls at 1 ms each is 20 ms, but the same 20 calls across regions at 100 ms each is 2 seconds.

sections.heading: From QPS to server count
sections.body: Interviewers often ask 'how many servers?' You need per-machine ballparks, stated as assumptions because they vary by 10x with hardware and workload. A stateless web or API server doing light work: roughly 1,000 to 10,000 requests per second. A single Redis node: on the order of 100,000 simple operations per second. A single relational database node: low thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries per second, much less for heavy joins. A single Kafka broker: hundreds of MB per second of throughput. Then apply the formula: servers = peak QPS / (per-server QPS x target utilization). Run at 50 to 60 percent target utilization so you have headroom for spikes and deploys. Then add redundancy: if you run across 3 availability zones and must survive losing one, the other two must carry everything, so you provision 1.5x. Example: 100,000 peak QPS, 2,000 QPS per server at 50% target (1,000 effective) is 100 servers, and 150 to survive a zone loss.

sections.heading: The estimation routine (say it out loud)
sections.body: 1) State assumptions: users, DAU, actions per user, read:write ratio, record size, retention. 2) Daily volume, then QPS average and peak. 3) Storage per day, then per year, then multiplied by replication (usually 3) and overhead (indexes, metadata, compaction, roughly 1.3x to 2x). 4) Bandwidth if media is involved. 5) Memory for the cache: cache the hot working set, often 10 to 20 percent of the daily read data. 6) The 'so what' sentence: what the numbers rule in and rule out. Spend about five minutes total, round aggressively, and never silently change an assumption. If the interviewer corrects one, recompute out loud.

key_terms.definition: Queries (requests) per second. Daily volume divided by about 10^5 as a quick estimate.
Ratio of peak to average load. 2x to 3x for steady traffic, 10x or more for spiky traffic.
The fraction of a server's max capacity you plan to use, usually 50 to 60 percent, to leave headroom.
Number of copies stored. Raw storage is multiplied by RF, commonly 3.
The subset of data actively read. This is what a cache needs to hold.
Data leaving a cloud provider's network. Often a major cost.
A factor of 10. Interviews care about being within one.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: You computed 6 TB. Is that a lot of data?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: No. A single modern server can hold tens of TB, so capacity is not the constraint. With replication factor 3 it is about 18 TB, still modest. The real constraints are the write rate, availability, and read latency. I'd say that capacity does not force sharding here, but the 70,000 peak writes per second might.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why design for peak instead of average?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Failures happen at peak. If I size for average, every spike causes queueing, timeouts, and retries that make it worse. I size for peak with headroom, and use autoscaling so I'm not paying for peak capacity at 3am, while keeping a floor that survives losing an availability zone.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: You said 100 servers. Utilization will be 20 percent at night. Isn't that wasteful?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Yes, so I'd autoscale the stateless tier on load, with a minimum floor for zone redundancy. The stateful tier scales less elastically, so I provision that closer to peak and accept some idle cost for safety.

say_it_out_loud: One thousand bytes is a kilobyte, a million is a megabyte, a billion is a gigabyte, a trillion is a terabyte.
A million events a day is about twelve per second. A billion is about twelve thousand per second.
Average is about forty thousand writes per second. I'll design for roughly a hundred and twenty thousand at peak.
That means a single database node won't cut it, so I'm partitioning the data.

drill.q: 3 billion requests per day. Average QPS and peak?
drill.a: 3 x 10^9 / 10^5 = about 30,000 average (exact about 35,000). Peak at 3x is about 100,000.

drill.q: 20 million photos per day at 3 MB each. Storage per day and per year?
drill.a: 2 x 10^7 x 3 x 10^6 = 6 x 10^13 bytes = 60 TB per day. 60 TB x 365 is about 21,900 TB, about 22 PB per year.

drill.q: 100,000 peak QPS, 2,000 QPS per server max, 50% target utilization, must survive losing 1 of 3 zones. How many servers?
drill.a: 1,000 effective per server gives 100 servers, times 1.5 for zone loss gives 150.

drill.q: 100,000 requests per second at 20 KB each. Bandwidth in Gbps?
drill.a: 2 x 10^9 bytes per second x 8 = 16 Gbps.

drill.q: 100 million user profiles at 1 KB. How much memory to cache all of them?
drill.a: 10^8 x 10^3 = 10^11 bytes = 100 GB, a handful of cache nodes.

drill.q: A page makes 20 sequential calls to a service. Same data center (0.5 ms) vs another continent (150 ms)?
drill.a: Same data center: about 10 ms. Other continent: about 3 seconds. Never put cross-region calls in a sequential loop.

drill.q: 800 GB per day for a year, with RF 3 and 1.5x overhead. Total raw storage?
4 trillion bytes. Units?

sessions.title: The request path: DNS, CDNs, load balancers, real-time protocols, API design
sessions.goal: Trace a request from phone to database and name every component, protocol, and failure mode on the way. Fix the webhook vs WebSocket confusion permanently.
sessions.warmup_note: 5 minutes. Answer out loud, then check.

warmup.q: 500 million events per day. Average per second?
warmup.a: 5 x 10^8 / 10^5 = about 5,000 per second (exact about 5,800).

warmup.q: 100,000 QPS peak, 1,000 effective QPS per server. Servers, and with zone-loss redundancy across 3 zones?
warmup.a: 100 servers, 150 with zone redundancy.

warmup.q: How many TB is 8 x 10^12 bytes?
warmup.a: 8 TB.

sections.heading: The request path end to end
sections.body: Walk through a request out loud in order. 1) The client resolves the domain through DNS, which can return different IPs by region (geo-DNS) or use anycast so the same IP routes to the nearest location. DNS answers are cached according to a TTL, so changing them is slow, which matters for failover. 2) Static content is served by a CDN edge node near the user. 3) Dynamic requests reach a load balancer, which terminates TLS and spreads requests over a pool of servers. 4) An API gateway may handle authentication, rate limiting, and routing. 5) Stateless application servers run business logic. 6) They talk to a cache, then a database, and enqueue background work on a queue. Naming every hop in this order is already a senior habit, because it shows you know where latency and failure live.

sections.heading: Load balancers in depth
sections.body: A Layer 4 balancer works on TCP/UDP connections using IP and port. It is very fast, cannot read HTTP, and is a good front door for raw connections including WebSockets. A Layer 7 balancer understands HTTP, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry safely, and add headers. NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, and cloud application load balancers are Layer 7. Algorithms: round robin, least connections (better when request cost varies), and hash-based (the same key goes to the same server, useful for cache locality). Health checks remove unhealthy servers: active checks probe an endpoint, passive checks watch real traffic for errors. Connection draining lets in-flight requests finish before a server is removed during a deploy. The load balancer is itself a single point of failure, so it is deployed redundantly, often as a managed service that spans zones. Avoid sticky sessions where you can, because they make load uneven and complicate failover. Prefer stateless servers with session data in a shared store or a signed token.

sections.heading: Real-time communication: pick the right tool
sections.body: Short polling: the client asks every few seconds. Simple, wasteful, delayed. Long polling: the server holds the request until data arrives, then the client asks again. Works through any proxy, costs a connection per client. Server-Sent Events (SSE): a one-way server-to-client stream over HTTP, ideal for live feeds, tickers, and progress bars. WebSocket: a persistent, two-way connection on a single TCP connection, started by an HTTP upgrade. Use it for chat, collaboration, and games. A webhook is a different category entirely: it is one server calling another server's URL when an event occurs, such as a payment provider notifying your backend. It is not persistent and it does not involve end-user clients. One-line rule: webhook is server-to-server callback, WebSocket is persistent client-server channel.

sections.heading: Scaling WebSockets (what a senior engineer adds)
sections.body: WebSocket servers are stateful because each connection lives on one machine. Each connection costs memory and a file descriptor, and one well-tuned server can hold on the order of hundreds of thousands of idle connections, so you often size by connection count, not request rate. You need a connection registry (for example a Redis map of user ID to gateway server) so other services know where to deliver a message, and a pub/sub layer or direct service-to-gateway routing to push to the right gateway. You need heartbeats (ping/pong) to detect dead connections, and reconnect logic on the client with exponential backoff plus jitter. Without jitter, a gateway crash or deploy causes a reconnect storm where every client returns at the same instant. Plan deploys with connection draining and gradual rollouts. Offline users get a push notification through the platform services (APNs for iOS, FCM for Android) and sync missed messages when they reconnect.

sections.heading: API design decisions
sections.body: REST is the default for public, resource-oriented APIs and plays well with HTTP caching. gRPC (binary, schema-first, HTTP/2) is common between internal services for lower overhead and streaming. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need, at the cost of harder caching and query-cost control. Pagination: offset pagination (page 5 of results) gets slow on big tables and shows duplicates or skips when data changes during paging. Cursor pagination (give me items after this cursor, where the cursor encodes the last seen ID or timestamp) is stable and fast, which is why you proposed it for chat history. Idempotency: GET, PUT, and DELETE are naturally idempotent. POST is not, so anything that creates something (a payment, an order) should accept an idempotency key so a retry returns the original result. Also mention versioning, rate limits per client, and that responses should be small: send IDs and fetch details separately if you can.

sections.heading: CDNs in depth
sections.body: A CDN caches content at edge locations. Pull mode: the CDN fetches from your origin on the first request and caches it for a TTL. Push mode: you upload content ahead of time, good for large known files. The cache key (usually the URL plus selected headers) decides what counts as the same object. Cache-Control headers tell the CDN and browsers how long to keep things. Invalidation is hard, so the common trick is versioned URLs (app.v123.js) so you never need to invalidate. An origin shield adds a mid-tier cache to reduce load on your origin. Private media uses signed, expiring URLs. Do not cache personalized responses without care. The metric that matters is hit ratio: at 95 percent, your origin sees 5 percent of traffic, and that directly sets your origin sizing and egress cost.

sections.heading: Stateless scaling and connection pooling
sections.body: Stateless servers are the free scaling lever: add machines behind the load balancer, remove them freely, replace them during deploys. State lives in the database, cache, queues, and the WebSocket layer. A practical trap: each server opens database connections, and a database has a connection limit (Postgres handles hundreds, not tens of thousands, comfortably). Scaling app servers from 20 to 400 can exhaust the database even though CPU is fine. The fix is a connection pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy) and bounded pool sizes per server. Also know TCP vs UDP: TCP is reliable and ordered, UDP is faster with no guarantees (used for video, gaming, and QUIC/HTTP3). HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection, and keep-alive avoids paying a new handshake for each request.

key_terms.definition: Multiple locations advertise the same IP and routing sends users to the nearest.
The point where encrypted traffic is decrypted, usually at the load balancer.
L4 balances TCP/UDP connections. L7 understands HTTP and can route by path or header.
Letting in-flight requests finish before removing a server.
Persistent two-way client-server channel over one TCP connection.
Server-to-server HTTP callback triggered by an event.
Many clients reconnecting simultaneously after an outage. Mitigated with jittered backoff.
Paging by a stable marker (last ID/timestamp) rather than an offset.
A client-supplied unique ID so retried writes are applied once.
Fraction of requests served from cache.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Your WebSocket gateway with 500,000 connections crashes. What happens?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Clients detect the dropped connection and reconnect. Without protection, all 500,000 reconnect at once and overload the other gateways, so clients use exponential backoff with jitter. On reconnect, each client sends the ID of its last received message so the server replays what it missed from durable storage. The connection registry entries expire by TTL. I'd also keep per-gateway connection counts below a cap so losing one node cannot overload the rest.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why not just use polling? It is simpler.
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: For low scale or infrequent updates, polling is fine and simpler to operate. For chat, polling every second at 100 million users is 100 million requests per second of mostly empty responses. A persistent connection amortizes the handshake and delivers immediately. I'd choose WebSocket here and keep long polling as a fallback for restrictive networks.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why cursor over offset pagination?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Offset requires the database to scan and skip N rows, so deep pages get slow, and if new items arrive while the user is paging, items shift and the user sees duplicates or misses some. A cursor on an indexed column like (timestamp, id) does a direct index seek and is stable.

say_it_out_loud: For real-time messaging I'll use WebSockets, since we need a persistent two-way connection. A webhook would be for server-to-server callbacks.
I'll put an L7 load balancer in front of the API tier so I can route by path and terminate TLS, with health checks and connection draining.
Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and resume from their last received message ID.
Static assets go behind a CDN with versioned URLs, so I never need cache invalidation.

drill.q: A payment provider needs to notify your server a charge succeeded.
drill.a: Webhook. It is a server-to-server callback. Verify its signature and handle retries idempotently.

drill.q: A live score ticker where the client only receives data.
drill.a: SSE (simpler than WebSocket), or WebSocket.

drill.q: You scale app servers from 20 to 400 and the database falls over with CPU idle. Why?
drill.a: Connection exhaustion. Add a connection pooler and cap pool sizes.

drill.q: Which load balancer layer routes /api to one pool and /images to another?
drill.a: Layer 7.

drill.q: How do you avoid ever invalidating CDN cached JavaScript?
drill.a: Versioned or content-hashed filenames, so each deploy uses new URLs.

drill.q: Why is a user pinned to one WebSocket server a problem for delivery?
drill.a: Other servers do not hold that user's connection, so you need a connection registry and pub/sub or routing to reach the right gateway.

sessions.title: Storage and caching: choosing from the numbers
sessions.goal: Choose a data store by running a checklist on the numbers, justify it with a trade-off, and design a cache that protects the database.
sessions.warmup_note: 5 minutes. Answer out loud, then check.

warmup.q: 100,000 requests per second, 20 KB each. Gbps?
warmup.a: 16 Gbps (2 GB per second x 8).

warmup.q: Webhook or WebSocket for a server-to-server payment notification?
warmup.a: Webhook.

warmup.q: Why does cursor pagination beat offset pagination?
warmup.a: It uses an index seek instead of scanning and skipping rows, and it stays stable when data changes while paging.

sections.heading: The checklist that fights the SQL default
sections.body: Your baseline review said you gravitated to PostgreSQL out of comfort even when the math pointed elsewhere. The fix is a fixed order of questions you answer before you name any database. 1) What are the peak writes per second? 2) How much data in total after retention, and after replication? 3) What are the access patterns: lookup by key, range scan by time, joins, aggregations, full-text search? 4) What consistency do I need: multi-row transactions, unique constraints, or is eventual consistency fine? 5) What latency does the user need? Only after these five do you map to a store. Equally important: the checklist also fights the opposite bias, choosing NoSQL because it sounds scalable. Plenty of correct designs are plain Postgres.

sections.heading: Relational databases (Postgres, MySQL)
sections.body: Choose when data is relational, you need transactions, unique constraints, and flexible queries, and the scale fits. A single well-provisioned node, plus read replicas, plus a cache, carries far more load than most people assume. Know the mechanics. An index is typically a B-tree, giving lookups in logarithmic time with very high fan-out, so even a billion rows is only 3 to 4 levels deep. A composite index on (a, b) serves queries on a, and on a and b together, but not b alone. A covering index contains every column the query needs, avoiding a table lookup. Indexes speed reads and slow writes, and each one costs storage, so index what you query. Read replicas scale reads but not writes, and they lag. Vertical scaling (bigger machine) is underrated and simple. The limits: write throughput on one primary, storage per node in the multi-terabyte range, and operational pain once you shard.

sections.heading: Key-value and wide-column stores (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
sections.body: Choose when write volume is very high, access is by key, and you do not need joins or multi-row transactions. You model the tables around your queries, not around entities. The partition key decides which node stores the data, and a clustering key sorts rows within a partition, so a table keyed by (conversation_id, message_id) lets you read the latest N messages for a conversation as one sequential read. You usually denormalize and write the same data into several tables, one per query. Pitfalls: hot partitions when one key gets disproportionate traffic, partitions that grow without bound (cap them with time buckets), secondary indexes that are expensive or limited, and limited ad hoc querying. In exchange you get near-linear horizontal scaling and high write throughput.

sections.heading: Other stores and when each appears
sections.body: Document stores (MongoDB) fit nested, flexible-schema records fetched whole. Search engines (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) hold inverted indexes for full-text search and filtering, and are fed from the primary database rather than being the source of truth. Object storage (S3) holds large immutable blobs cheaply and durably, with higher latency; you keep metadata in a database and serve through a CDN, and clients upload directly with presigned URLs so files never pass through your app servers. Data warehouses and columnar stores (BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse) handle analytics over huge scans and are kept separate from the transactional database, fed by change data capture or batch loads. Using the right store per job is called polyglot persistence, and it is normal.

sections.heading: Caching in depth
sections.body: Where caches live: browser, CDN, an in-process cache inside each server (fastest, but each server has its own copy), a distributed cache like Redis (shared, one network hop), and the database's own buffer pool. Patterns: cache-aside (read cache, on miss read the DB and fill the cache) is the default because the app controls it and cache failures degrade instead of break. Write-through keeps the cache fresh at the cost of slower writes. Write-back is fast but risks losing data if the cache fails. Invalidation is the hard part: use TTLs as a backstop, delete or update the key on writes, or publish change events. Known failure modes: cache stampede when a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database (fixes: a lock so one request rebuilds it, request coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs, or refreshing early); the hot key problem where one key saturates one cache shard (fixes: a small in-process cache in front, or replicating the key across shards); cache penetration from requests for keys that do not exist (fix: cache the negative result briefly, or use a Bloom filter); and cold start after a cache restart (fix: warm it, or throttle database load).

sections.heading: Hit-ratio math that justifies a cache
sections.body: Average latency = hit_ratio x cache_latency + (1 - hit_ratio) x database_latency. More important is load: the database only sees the misses. At 100,000 reads per second, a 90 percent hit ratio sends 10,000 reads per second to the database, while 99 percent sends 1,000. Going from 90 to 99 percent cuts database load by 10x, which is why small improvements in hit ratio matter. To size a cache, estimate the hot working set. Often about 20 percent of items account for about 80 percent of reads, so cache that 20 percent, not everything. Example: 100 million items at 1 KB is 100 GB total, and caching the hot 20 percent needs about 20 GB, which fits in one or two Redis nodes. Say: 'I'd cache the hot 20 percent, about 20 GB, with LRU eviction and a 24 hour TTL, targeting a 95 percent hit ratio.'

sections.heading: Redis specifics worth knowing
sections.body: Redis executes commands on a single thread per instance, so each operation is atomic and fast, and you scale by sharding. Redis Cluster divides the key space into 16,384 hash slots spread over the nodes. Data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets (leaderboards, time-ordered feeds), HyperLogLog (approximate unique counts), and streams. Persistence is optional: RDB snapshots and an append-only file (AOF). Eviction policies include allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl, and others. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes, which means Redis is excellent as a cache and acceptable for ephemeral data, but be careful using it as the only copy of important data.

sections.heading: Worked decision, spoken the senior way
sections.body: Requirement: 2 billion writes per day, 12 billion records at about 500 bytes, lookups by ID, no joins. Math: about 23,000 writes per second average, about 70,000 at peak, and 6 TB raw (about 18 TB with RF 3, more with overhead). Reasoning: a single Postgres primary would be strained at 70,000 writes per second and storage is at the uncomfortable end, and I never need joins, so the relational strengths are unused. I'd choose a wide-column or key-value store partitioned by ID. Trade-off: I give up joins and flexible queries and must know access patterns up front. Alternative I considered: sharded Postgres, which works but adds rebalancing and cross-shard complexity for no relational benefit. Trigger to revisit: if requirements add complex reporting, I'd stream into a warehouse instead of querying this store. Notice the shape: numbers, decision, cost, rejected alternative, trigger to revisit.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why not just use Postgres with read replicas?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Read replicas scale reads, not writes. At 70,000 peak writes per second every write still lands on one primary, and 18 TB with replication is heavy for one node. I could shard Postgres, but then I own rebalancing and cross-shard queries without using joins. For this access pattern a partitioned key-value store is simpler to scale. If the volume were 1,000 writes per second, I'd choose Postgres without hesitation.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Your cache cluster restarts. What happens?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Every request misses and the database takes the full read load, which it was never sized for. Mitigations: keep replicas of cache shards so a single failure is not a full flush, throttle or queue database reads, warm the cache from recent hot keys before taking traffic, and use request coalescing so concurrent misses for the same key produce one database read.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How do you keep the cache consistent with the database?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: I accept bounded staleness and set a TTL as a backstop. On writes I update the database first, then delete the cache key (not update it), because deleting avoids racing writers leaving stale values. For data where staleness is unacceptable, such as inventory counts at checkout, I read from the database instead of the cache.

I'm giving up joins and ad hoc queries. I considered sharded Postgres and rejected it because I'd pay the operational cost without using relational features.
I'll cache the hot twenty percent with cache-aside, LRU eviction, and a TTL, targeting a ninety-five percent hit ratio.

sections.heading: How to run this session
sections.body: Open a fresh chat with your AI, paste the mock prompt template from this file, and paste the prompt below. Stand up and talk. Use dictation so you get a transcript. Do not look at the notes in this session while the clock runs. When you finish, paste the transcript and the AI's scores into the System Design note tab as 'Mock 1', then write three lines yourself: what I got wrong, what terms I missed, what I'd do differently. Your own three lines matter more than the AI's grade.

sections.heading: What a strong answer contains
sections.body: Requirements: shortening, redirect, custom aliases, expiry, analytics (async), and abuse protection. Numbers: about 1,200 writes per second, 115,000 reads per second, 18 TB per year, so the system is read-heavy and storage is modest. Design: stateless app servers behind an L7 load balancer, a Redis cache with cache-aside, and a key-value store partitioned by short code. Deep dive: how short codes are generated and how you guarantee uniqueness. Closing: monitoring, abuse, and failure modes.

sections.heading: Key generation options you must be able to compare
sections.body: Base62 uses a-z, A-Z, 0-9, so 7 characters give 62^7, about 3.5 trillion codes. Over 5 years you need about 180 billion (100M x 365 x 5), so 7 characters is enough with room to spare. Option 1: hash the URL (MD5/SHA) and take the first 7 base62 characters. Stateless and the same URL maps to the same code, but collisions occur (birthday paradox) so you must check and retry, and deduplication by URL conflicts with per-user aliases. Option 2: a global counter encoded in base62. No collisions, but a single counter is a bottleneck and a single point of failure, and codes are guessable and enumerable. Fix by giving each app server a range (say 1 million IDs) from a coordination service, so servers allocate locally. Option 3: a pre-generated key service that hands out unused random keys, which avoids predictability and removes collision handling from the hot path. Option 4: Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (timestamp, machine, sequence), which are unique without coordination but encode to about 11 base62 characters, longer than 7. Pick one and defend it. A reasonable senior choice: range-allocated counters with a reversible scramble so codes are not sequential, or a key service.

sections.heading: Redirect semantics, expiry, and analytics
sections.body: A 301 (permanent) redirect is cached by browsers, which reduces your load but hides repeat clicks from your analytics. A 302 (temporary) hits your server every time, which gives accurate analytics and lets you change or expire links. State which you choose and why. Expiry: store expires_at, check it on read, and delete lazily or with a background sweeper. Custom aliases need an atomic 'insert if not exists' (a conditional write or unique constraint), because two users could claim the same alias at once. Analytics must not slow the redirect: publish a click event to a queue and aggregate asynchronously. Abuse: rate limit creation per user and IP, scan destinations against a known-bad list, and never follow the destination URL server-side without care (SSRF risk).

mock.prompt: Design a URL shortening service like bit.ly. Users submit a long URL and receive a short one. Visiting the short URL redirects to the original. Assume a large consumer scale.

clock.what_to_do: Ask about custom aliases, expiry, analytics, and who can create links. Then state: 100M new URLs per day, 100:1 read to write, retention 5 years, redirect latency under 100 ms, 99.9 percent availability.

About 1,200 writes per second, about 115,000 reads per second, 500 bytes per record so about 18 TB per year and 90 TB over 5 years. Say the so-what: read-heavy, storage is modest, so cache hard and partition by code.
POST /shorten (long URL, optional alias, optional expiry, idempotency key). GET /{code} returns 302. Record: code (key), long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at. Access is by key only.

L7 load balancer, stateless app servers, Redis cache-aside with LRU, key-value store partitioned by code and replicated across zones, queue for click events, key service or range allocator. Draw the redirect path and the create path separately.
Key generation and uniqueness (compare 3 options, pick one). Then cache behavior: sizing the hot 20 percent, hot keys for viral links, and what happens when the cache fails.
Bottlenecks, monitoring (hit ratio, p99 redirect latency, error rate, key-range exhaustion), abuse handling, and the next 10x step.

pressure_questions.q: A celebrity tweets one of your links and it gets 200,000 requests per second. What breaks first?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: A single hot key. The cache shard holding it saturates. I add a small in-process cache with a short TTL on every app server so most requests never reach Redis, and I serve through a CDN if the redirect is cacheable. The database is protected because the key is already cached.

pressure_questions.q: How do you guarantee two users never get the same code?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Allocation is the uniqueness mechanism. With range-allocated counters, each server owns a disjoint range so collisions are impossible by construction. For custom aliases I use an atomic conditional insert on the key, and return a conflict if it exists.

pressure_questions.q: The cache cluster goes down. Walk me through it.
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Reads fall through to the database, which sees 115,000 per second instead of about 6,000. It cannot take that. So I need protection: cache replicas so one node loss is not a flush, request coalescing, rate limiting or load shedding at the app tier, and a fallback that serves from a local cache. I'd also alert on hit ratio dropping.

pressure_questions.q: How would you count clicks without slowing redirects?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Publish a click event to a queue asynchronously, off the critical path, and aggregate in a stream processor into per-link counters. If the queue is unavailable I drop or buffer locally, because accurate analytics are less important than redirect availability.

sessions.title: Partitioning, replication, and consistent hashing in depth
sessions.goal: Explain how data is split and copied across machines, what goes wrong (hot spots, lag, split brain), and how each fix works.
sessions.warmup_note: 5 minutes. Answer out loud, then check.

warmup.q: 100,000 reads per second at a 99% cache hit ratio. Database load?
warmup.a: 1,000 reads per second.

warmup.q: 100,000 peak QPS, 1,000 effective QPS per server, survive losing 1 of 3 zones. Servers?
warmup.a: 100 normally, 150 with zone redundancy.

warmup.q: A composite index on (a, b). Does a query filtering only on b use it well?
warmup.a: No. Only filters that start with a use it.

sections.heading: Two tools, almost always used together
sections.body: Partitioning (sharding) splits data so each machine holds a slice. It scales capacity and write throughput. Replication keeps copies of each slice on several machines. It scales read throughput and provides availability and durability. Replication does not scale writes, because every replica still has to apply every write. Real systems do both: the data is divided into partitions and each partition is replicated, for example 3 copies in 3 zones. Say this structure out loud when you describe any large store, because it signals you understand what each mechanism buys you.

sections.heading: Partitioning strategies and hot spots
sections.body: Hash partitioning applies a hash to the key so data spreads evenly, at the cost of efficient range queries. Range partitioning keeps adjacent keys together, which is good for scans but creates hot spots when keys are sequential (partition by timestamp and all current writes hit one shard). Directory-based partitioning uses a lookup service mapping keys to shards, which is flexible but adds a dependency. Most large systems combine them: hash on a partition key to pick the node, then sort by a clustering key inside it. A good shard key has high cardinality, even distribution, and matches the dominant query so that most requests touch one partition. Skew still happens: a celebrity account, a viral post, a giant tenant. Mitigations: split the hot partition, add a random suffix to spread one logical key across several physical keys (and read all of them), cache the hot key, or route known heavy hitters to dedicated capacity. Name the hot-spot risk of your own shard key before the interviewer does.

sections.heading: Consistent hashing, virtual nodes, and fixed partitions
sections.body: With hash(key) mod N, adding a server remaps most keys: going from 4 to 5 servers moves about 80 percent of keys, which for a cache means a near-total flush. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next server clockwise. Adding a server only takes keys from its neighbor, so about 1/N of keys move (about 20 percent going from 4 to 5). Plain rings balance poorly, so each physical server owns many virtual nodes (often 100 or more) scattered around the ring, which evens out load and lets stronger machines own more. Replication on a ring: store each key on the next R distinct physical nodes clockwise. A closely related and very common alternative is a fixed number of partitions created up front, much larger than the number of nodes (Kafka partitions, Elasticsearch shards, Redis Cluster's 16,384 slots). Adding a node means moving whole partitions to it. This is simpler to operate than a pure ring, but you must choose the partition count carefully because changing it later is painful. Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing is another approach that gets the same minimal movement without a ring.

sections.heading: Rebalancing and operations
sections.body: Moving data between nodes consumes network and disk and competes with live traffic, so rebalancing is throttled and often triggered by an operator, not fully automatic. A fully automatic scheme can cascade: a slow node looks dead, its data moves to others, which become overloaded and look dead too. State this when asked about adding capacity: you add the node, rebalance gradually in the background, and watch latency while it runs.

sections.heading: Replication models
sections.body: Single-leader: all writes go to one leader that streams a log to followers. Simple and consistent, with the leader as a write bottleneck and a failover event. Multi-leader: several nodes accept writes (often one per region), which gives low write latency everywhere but requires conflict resolution. Leaderless (Dynamo-style, Cassandra): any replica accepts writes, clients write to W replicas and read from R, and conflicts are repaired later. Synchronous replication waits for follower acknowledgment before confirming a write, which prevents data loss but adds latency and reduces availability. Asynchronous replication confirms immediately and risks losing the last few writes if the leader dies. Semi-synchronous waits for one follower, a common compromise. The replication log can be statement-based, physical (WAL shipping), or logical (row changes), and logical logs are what enable change data capture.

sections.heading: Replication lag anomalies and their fixes
sections.body: With asynchronous followers, reads from a follower can be stale, which causes specific user-visible bugs. Read-your-writes violation: you post a comment, refresh, and it is gone because the read hit a lagging replica. Fix: route a user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or track the last write position (log sequence number) and only read from replicas that have caught up. Monotonic reads violation: you see newer data, refresh, and see older data because you hit a different replica. Fix: pin each user to one replica. Consistent prefix violation: you see an answer before the question because the writes were replicated out of order across partitions. Fix: keep causally related writes in the same partition or track causality. These are good vocabulary to drop because they show you know what eventual consistency feels like to a user.

sections.heading: Failover, split brain, and fencing
sections.body: Failover steps: detect that the leader is down (heartbeats and timeouts, which can be wrong), choose a new leader (usually the most up-to-date follower, through an election), and reconfigure clients. Hazards: with async replication the new leader may be missing recent writes, so those writes are lost or conflict. Split brain occurs when the old leader is only partitioned, not dead, and two nodes both believe they are the leader and accept writes. Fencing prevents this: each new leader gets a higher epoch or fencing token, and storage or followers reject writes from older epochs. The timeout is a trade-off: too short causes false failovers during a latency spike, too long extends downtime.

sections.heading: Secondary indexes, cross-partition queries, and quorums
sections.body: If data is partitioned by user_id and you also query by email, you need a secondary index. A local index (each partition indexes its own data) makes writes cheap but queries must scatter to all partitions and gather, which is slow and hurts tail latency. A global index is itself partitioned by the indexed term, making queries fast but writes touch multiple partitions and the index is updated asynchronously. Joins across partitions are expensive, so denormalize or pre-join at write time. For leaderless quorums with N replicas: a write succeeds after W acknowledgments, a read queries R replicas, and if R + W > N the read set overlaps the latest write set. With N=3, W=2, R=2 works. Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff accept writes on stand-in nodes during failures and hand them back later, favoring availability. Read repair and anti-entropy (comparing Merkle trees of data) heal divergent replicas.

key_terms.definition: The attribute that decides which partition holds a record.
A partition receiving disproportionate load.
Ring-based assignment where adding or removing a node moves about 1/N of keys.
Many ring positions per physical node, for balance.
Delay before followers reflect the leader's writes.
A guarantee that you see your own recent writes.
Two nodes both believing they are the leader.
A monotonically increasing number that lets storage reject writes from stale leaders.
The number of replicas that must respond. R + W > N guarantees overlap.
A stand-in node holds writes for a down replica and delivers them later.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Your database leader dies. Walk me through what happens to in-flight writes.
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Writes acknowledged by the leader but not yet replicated may be lost with asynchronous replication. A follower is elected, ideally the most caught-up one, clients are redirected, and I use an epoch or fencing token so the old leader cannot accept writes if it comes back. If losing those writes is unacceptable, I use synchronous or semi-synchronous replication to at least one follower and accept the added write latency.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: A single celebrity account is overloading its partition. What do you do?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: First confirm with metrics that it is a hot key. Then reduce load on that key: cache it, split it across multiple suffixed keys so reads and writes fan out across partitions, and handle known heavy hitters through a separate path with dedicated capacity. I would not change the whole sharding scheme for one outlier.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why not add more replicas to scale writes?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Replicas each apply every write, so more replicas increase total write work and replication lag. Replication scales reads and availability. Writes scale by partitioning, so I'd add partitions.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How would you query by a field that is not the shard key?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Either a global secondary index partitioned by that field, updated asynchronously (fast queries, slightly stale), or scatter-gather across all partitions (simple, slow at scale). For a heavy query pattern I'd maintain a second table keyed by that field, written at the same time as the main one.

say_it_out_loud: I'll partition by user ID with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, so adding a node only moves about one-Nth of the data.
Each partition has three replicas across zones, with semi-synchronous replication to one follower so we don't lose acknowledged writes.
Reads that follow a write go to the leader for a few seconds to preserve read-your-writes.
The hot-spot risk is a single huge account, which I'd handle with key splitting and caching.

drill.q: hash mod 4 changes to hash mod 5. Fraction of keys that move?
drill.a: About 80 percent. Consistent hashing moves about 20 percent.

drill.q: Why is partitioning by timestamp risky for a write-heavy table?
drill.a: All current writes land on the newest partition, creating a hot spot.

drill.q: N=5. Choose W and R for strong overlap with fast reads.
drill.a: W=3, R=3 (R+W=6 > 5). Or W=5, R=1 for fast reads but writes need all nodes.

drill.q: User posts and immediately refreshes, post missing. Name the anomaly and a fix.
drill.a: Read-your-writes violation. Route their reads to the leader briefly, or only read from replicas that have caught up to their last write position.

drill.q: Why is global failover timeout tuning a trade-off?
drill.a: Short timeouts cause false failovers during latency spikes. Long timeouts extend real downtime.

drill.q: Why use more partitions than nodes?
drill.a: It makes rebalancing simple: you move whole partitions to a new node instead of splitting data.

sessions.title: Asynchronous systems: queues, Kafka, delivery semantics, back-pressure, outbox
sessions.goal: Choose between queue, log, and pub/sub; explain delivery guarantees and idempotency; design for overload with back-pressure.
sessions.warmup_note: 5 minutes. Answer out loud, then check.

warmup.q: Why does adding replicas not improve write throughput?
warmup.a: Every replica applies every write. Partitioning scales writes.

warmup.q: Name the anomaly: you see newer data, refresh, then see older data.
warmup.a: Monotonic reads violation. Fix by pinning a user to one replica.

warmup.q: 4 to 5 nodes with consistent hashing. About what fraction of keys moves?
warmup.a: About 1/5, roughly 20 percent.

sections.heading: Why go asynchronous, and what it costs
sections.body: Asynchronous messaging decouples producers from consumers in time and in failure. Benefits: the user-facing request returns fast because slow work (email, image processing, analytics) happens later; spikes are absorbed by the queue (load leveling) instead of crashing downstream services; one event can fan out to many consumers; and a consumer outage does not break the producer. Costs: eventual consistency (the result is not visible immediately), duplicates, ordering challenges, harder debugging, and a new component to operate. A senior answer states both sides: 'I'm putting this behind a queue so the API returns in 50 ms, and in exchange the user sees the result a few seconds later and consumers must be idempotent.'

sections.heading: Three shapes: queue, log, pub/sub
sections.body: A work queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) delivers each message to one of many competing consumers, then deletes it after acknowledgment. If a consumer does not acknowledge before the visibility timeout, the message reappears, which gives at-least-once delivery. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) collects messages that fail repeatedly so a poison message does not block the line. Standard SQS gives high throughput with best-effort ordering, FIFO queues give ordering per message group at lower throughput. A log (Kafka) is an append-only, partitioned, replicated record of events retained for a configured time. Consumers track their own offset, so many independent consumer groups can read the same data, and any group can rewind and replay. Pub/sub (SNS, Redis pub/sub, Google Pub/Sub) delivers each message to every subscriber of a topic. Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget with no persistence, which is fine for ephemeral signals like 'tell the other gateway' but not for anything that must not be lost.

sections.heading: Kafka mechanics you should be able to explain
sections.body: A topic is split into partitions. A producer chooses the partition, usually by hashing a key, so all events with the same key land in the same partition and keep their order. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. Within a consumer group, each partition is consumed by at most one consumer, so the partition count is the ceiling on parallelism: a topic with 12 partitions and 20 consumers in one group leaves 8 consumers idle. Each partition has a leader and replicas, and the replication factor is commonly 3. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write is acknowledged only when enough replicas have it, which trades latency for durability. Consumers commit offsets; if a consumer crashes it resumes from the last committed offset, so any messages processed after the last commit are processed again. Rebalancing when consumers join or leave pauses consumption briefly. Log compaction keeps only the latest record per key, useful for changelog-style topics. Retention lets you replay history, for example to rebuild a search index or fix a consumer bug.

sections.heading: Delivery semantics and idempotency
sections.body: At-most-once: send and never retry, so you may lose messages. At-least-once: retry until acknowledged, so you may duplicate. Exactly-once delivery across a network is not achievable in general; what you can get is exactly-once effect by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing. Kafka offers idempotent producers and transactions that give exactly-once semantics for read-process-write within Kafka, but the moment a consumer calls an external service or database, you are back to needing idempotency. Patterns: a dedupe table with a unique constraint on message ID (insert first, skip if it already exists), conditional writes (apply only if version matches), making operations naturally idempotent (set status = shipped, not increment a counter), and idempotency keys passed to downstream APIs. Always say 'at-least-once with idempotent consumers' when asked about reliability, and name how you dedupe.

sections.heading: Ordering
sections.body: Global ordering across a whole topic is expensive and limits throughput to one partition or one writer. Most systems only need per-entity ordering: all messages for one conversation, one account, or one order in sequence. Achieve that by using the entity ID as the partition key. Add a sequence number or version to messages so consumers can detect gaps, duplicates, and out-of-order delivery, and ignore stale updates. Retries can reorder messages (message 2 succeeds before message 1 is retried), so if order matters, stop processing a key until the earlier message succeeds, or use version checks.

sections.heading: Back-pressure, lag, and overload
sections.body: Consumer lag (how far the consumer is behind the head of the log) is the single most important queue metric. If producers write 50,000 messages per second and consumers process 40,000, lag grows by 10,000 per second, which is 36 million messages per hour. Responses: scale consumers (up to the partition count), make processing faster, or shed load. Use bounded queues so memory cannot grow without limit. Apply back-pressure so producers slow down when the system is saturated: rate limit producers, return 429 or 503 to clients, or drop low-priority work first (priority queues or separate queues for urgent and bulk traffic). Isolate slow or failing consumers so one bad dependency does not stall everything. For retries, use delayed retry queues with exponential backoff instead of immediately requeueing, and move poison messages to a DLQ with alerts so a human can inspect them.

sections.heading: The dual-write problem and the outbox pattern
sections.body: A service that updates its database and then publishes an event has two writes to two systems. If it crashes in between, the database changed but no event was sent (or the reverse), and downstream systems drift. The transactional outbox pattern solves this: in the same database transaction as the business change, insert an event row into an outbox table. A separate relay process (or change data capture such as Debezium reading the database log) reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, retrying until it succeeds. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers dedupe by event ID. Change data capture is also the clean way to keep caches, search indexes, and data warehouses in sync with the primary database without dual writes in application code.

Dead-letter queue for messages that repeatedly fail.
Set of consumers sharing the partitions of a topic.
A consumer's position in a partition.
How far behind consumers are from the newest messages.

Retaining only the latest record per key.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Your consumer crashes after processing a message but before committing the offset. What happens?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: On restart it resumes from the last committed offset and processes the message again. That is at-least-once delivery. The handler must be idempotent: I record the message ID in a table with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the side effect, so the second attempt is skipped.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How would you handle a message that always fails?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Retry a bounded number of times with exponential backoff using a delay topic or queue, so it does not block the partition. After the limit, move it to a dead-letter queue with the error and alert on DLQ depth. Someone fixes the bug or the data, then replays from the DLQ.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why Kafka rather than SQS for this?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: If several independent consumers need the same stream and I need replay and per-key ordering, Kafka fits. If it's one pool of workers processing independent jobs once, SQS is simpler and managed, with no partition planning. I'm choosing based on whether I need multiple consumer groups and replay.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Your service writes to Postgres then publishes to Kafka. What can go wrong?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: A crash between the two leaves the database updated with no event, or an event with no committed data. I'd use the outbox pattern: write the event in the same transaction, and have a relay or CDC publish it with retries, with consumers deduping by event ID.

say_it_out_loud: I'm putting this behind a queue so the API stays fast. In exchange, results are eventually consistent and consumers must be idempotent.
Events are keyed by conversation ID, so ordering is preserved per conversation, not globally.
Delivery is at-least-once, and each handler dedupes on message ID with a unique constraint.
I'd alert on consumer lag and scale consumers up to the partition count, and shed low-priority work if lag keeps growing.

drill.q: A topic has 12 partitions, one consumer group with 20 consumers. How many are active?

sections.heading: CAP, stated correctly
sections.body: CAP is often misquoted as 'pick two of three'. The accurate statement: when a network partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write, meaning linearizability) and availability (every request to a live node gets a response). You do not get to opt out of partitions, so the real choice only matters during a partition. PACELC extends this: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. This matters because even without partitions, stronger consistency costs latency, since replicas must coordinate. Examples: Dynamo-style stores are tunable and often lean toward availability and low latency. ZooKeeper and etcd choose consistency and will refuse to serve if they lose a majority. Spanner is consistent and is engineered for very high availability, with the cost paid in commit latency. In an interview, say 'for this feature I choose consistency over availability because...' rather than labeling a database CP or AP.

sections.heading: The consistency ladder
sections.body: Linearizable (strong): the system behaves as if there is one copy and operations take effect instantly at some point between request and response. Expensive: needs coordination, often through a leader or consensus. Sequential: all clients see operations in the same order, but not necessarily real-time order. Causal: if A could have influenced B, everyone sees A before B; unrelated events may appear in different orders. Session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes. Eventual: if writes stop, replicas eventually converge, with no promise about what you read in the meantime. Higher on the ladder means simpler reasoning for the application and higher latency and lower availability. Do not confuse this with ACID's 'C' and isolation: transaction isolation is about concurrent transactions on shared data, while CAP consistency is about replicas agreeing.

sections.heading: Pick consistency per feature
sections.body: The senior habit is to assign consistency by feature, not by system. Strong consistency where wrong answers cost money or correctness: account balances, inventory and seat reservations, unique usernames, payments, permissions. Causal or session consistency where users would notice anomalies: a chat conversation (replies after the message they answer), your own profile edits, your own posts. Eventual consistency where staleness is invisible: like counts, view counts, follower counts, search indexes, recommendation feeds, analytics. State it in the interview: 'Likes can be eventually consistent and counted asynchronously, but the seat reservation uses a conditional write on a single partition.' Then design the strong parts to be small: keep them on a single partition with a single writer so you do not need distributed coordination.

sections.heading: Time, clocks, and ordering
sections.body: Machine clocks drift and NTP corrections can make time jump, so wall-clock timestamps from different machines are not a reliable total order. Last-write-wins (LWW) using wall clocks can silently discard a newer write when a clock is behind. Logical clocks fix ordering without real time. A Lamport clock is a counter that each node increments and updates to max(local, received) + 1, giving an order consistent with causality (if A happened before B, A's timestamp is lower, but the reverse is not guaranteed). Vector clocks keep a counter per node and can tell whether two events are causally ordered or concurrent, which Dynamo-style systems use to detect conflicts. Hybrid logical clocks combine physical time with a logical counter. Google Spanner uses TrueTime, which exposes bounded clock uncertainty and waits out that uncertainty on commit to get external consistency. Practical advice: let a single owner assign order. A conversation's partition leader assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number to each message, which is far simpler than comparing clocks.

sections.heading: Unique ID generation
sections.body: Needs: unique, ideally roughly time-sortable (good for index locality and paging), generated without a central bottleneck. Random UUIDv4: unique, no coordination, but random inserts fragment B-tree indexes and it is not sortable by time. Time-ordered variants (UUIDv7, ULID) fix locality. Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs: 41 bits of millisecond timestamp, 10 bits of machine ID, 12 bits of sequence, which allows 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine, sortable, and compact. Risks: clock going backward on a machine (refuse to issue IDs until it catches up) and machine ID assignment (use a coordination service). Database auto-increment is simple but a bottleneck across shards, though ranges can be allocated per server. Ticket-server or range-allocation approaches hand out blocks of IDs.

sections.heading: Conflict resolution
sections.body: Conflicts happen when two replicas accept concurrent writes (multi-leader and leaderless systems, offline-capable clients). Options: avoid them with a single writer per key. Last-write-wins, which is simple and lossy. Application-level merge, where the system returns siblings and the app merges (the old Dynamo shopping cart merged by union). CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) are data structures designed so concurrent updates merge deterministically without coordination: counters, sets, registers, and sequences used in collaborative editing. Operational transformation is the older approach to collaborative text editing. Choose by data type: a counter or a set merges well, a bank balance does not, and that is why money gets a single writer.

sections.heading: Consensus and coordination
sections.body: Consensus protocols (Paxos, Raft, ZAB) let a group of nodes agree on a sequence of values despite failures, as long as a majority is alive. A cluster of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures, so 3 nodes tolerate 1 and 5 tolerate 2. A leader is elected, appends entries to a replicated log, and commits after a majority acknowledge. Cost: every committed write needs a majority round trip, so it is slow relative to a single node and it is unavailable without a majority. Use it for small, critical metadata: leader election, configuration, service discovery, locks, and the metadata of other systems. Systems built on it include etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, and the replication groups inside Spanner and CockroachDB. Do not put high-volume data through it. Distributed locks: a lock with a TTL is not safe on its own, because a client can pause (garbage collection, a network stall), its lock expires, and it resumes and writes while another client holds the lock. The fix is a fencing token, a number that increases with each lock grant, which the protected resource checks and uses to reject stale holders. Say this when someone proposes a Redis lock around a critical section.

key_terms.definition: Strongest single-object consistency: behaves like one copy with instant operations.
If partitioned choose A or C; else choose latency or consistency.
Causally related events are seen in order by everyone.
Replicas converge if updates stop, with no timing guarantee.
Logical counter ordering events consistent with causality.
Per-node counters that detect concurrent versus ordered events.
Last write wins. Simple, lossy, clock-dependent.
Data type whose concurrent updates merge deterministically.
64-bit time-sortable ID: 41 bits time, 10 bits machine, 12 bits sequence.
Consensus protocols for agreeing on a replicated log with majority quorums.
Increasing number issued with a lock so stale holders are rejected.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Two users try to book the last seat at the same instant. How do you prevent a double booking?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Make the seat's state change an atomic, conditional operation on a single partition: update seat set status=held where id=X and status=available, and check the affected row count. Only one succeeds. If the booking spans several resources I use a short-lived reservation (a hold with expiry) and confirm after payment. I would not rely on a cache or on eventually consistent replicas for this check.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why not use timestamps to order chat messages?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Client and server clocks drift and two messages can have the same millisecond, so timestamps are not a reliable total order. Instead the conversation's partition owner assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number as each message is accepted. Clients order by that sequence, and timestamps are for display only.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Someone suggests a Redis lock with a TTL to protect a critical section. Concerns?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: If the holder pauses longer than the TTL, the lock expires and a second holder enters while the first resumes, so both write. I would add a fencing token checked by the resource, or avoid the lock by using a conditional write or a single-writer design. For correctness-critical locks I'd use a consensus-based system such as etcd or ZooKeeper.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Is a like counter strongly consistent?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: No need. It can be eventually consistent. I'd buffer increments and aggregate them asynchronously, possibly with sharded counters to avoid a hot row, and accept that the displayed count is slightly stale.

say_it_out_loud: Account balances and seat reservations are strongly consistent on a single partition with conditional writes. Likes and view counts are eventually consistent.
Message order within a conversation comes from a sequence number assigned by the partition owner, not from timestamps.
A TTL lock isn't safe by itself, so I'd add a fencing token or use a conditional write instead.
For configuration and leader election I'd use etcd or ZooKeeper, but I wouldn't put data traffic through consensus.

drill.q: Classify: account balance, like count, username uniqueness, search index, chat order within a conversation.
drill.a: Balance: strong. Like count: eventual. Username uniqueness: strong. Search index: eventual. Chat order: per-conversation sequence (causal/sequential per conversation).

drill.q: Snowflake ID: how many IDs per millisecond per machine?
drill.a: 12 sequence bits = 4,096.

drill.q: 5-node Raft cluster. How many failures tolerated?
drill.a: 2 (a majority of 3 must be alive).

drill.q: Why is LWW dangerous with wall clocks?
drill.a: A node with a slow clock can have its newer write discarded in favor of an older one.

drill.q: What does PACELC add to CAP?
drill.a: Even without a partition, there is a latency vs consistency trade-off.

drill.q: Lamport vs vector clocks: which can detect concurrent writes?
drill.a: Vector clocks.

sections.heading: What changed since your baseline
sections.body: In your baseline you identified pagination and pub/sub on your own, which are good instincts. The gaps were: calling a WebSocket a webhook, not naming consistent hashing, saying 'it depends on the company', and a 1,000x storage slip. Today's goal is to hit those cleanly, then go further on what separates senior answers: delivery receipts, ordering, offline sync, and failure of a gateway.

sections.heading: What a strong answer contains
sections.body: Requirements: 1:1 and group chat, delivery and read receipts, history, offline delivery, presence, media. Numbers: about 46,000 messages per second average, 140,000 peak, about 800 GB per day, about 290 TB per year before replication. Architecture: clients connect by WebSocket through an L4 or L7 load balancer to stateless-ish gateway servers. A connection registry (user to gateway) lives in Redis. A chat service validates, assigns a per-conversation sequence number, persists the message, then routes it to recipients' gateways via pub/sub or direct service calls, and to a push service for offline users. Storage: a wide-column store keyed by (conversation_id) with clustering by sequence number, so loading history is one partition read. Media goes to object storage via presigned URLs, with thumbnails created asynchronously, served through a CDN.

sections.heading: Delivery, ordering, and sync (the deep dive)
sections.body: Persist before acknowledging: the server stores the message, then acks the sender ('sent'). Delivery is at-least-once, so the client sends a client-generated message ID and the server dedupes on it. The recipient's device acks receipt ('delivered'), then a read event ('read'), which are small state updates, not new messages. Ordering uses the per-conversation sequence number assigned by the partition owner. Offline sync: the client stores the highest sequence number it has per conversation and, on reconnect, requests everything after it, which is a range read on the partition. Group fan-out: for small groups, write once to the conversation and deliver to each member's gateway; for very large groups, avoid per-member writes and let members pull by sequence number. Presence: heartbeats set a key with a short TTL in Redis, and you only publish presence changes to the people who care (contacts viewing the chat), not to everyone. Hot partitions: a huge group chat makes one partition hot, handled with rate limits, slower sync paths, and splitting message history into time buckets inside the partition.

sections.heading: Failure modes you should raise yourself
sections.body: Gateway crash with hundreds of thousands of connections: clients reconnect with jittered exponential backoff and resume from their last sequence number, and registry entries expire by TTL. Chat service crash mid-send: the client retries with the same message ID and the server dedupes. Message store partition unavailable: replication across zones, and writes to a quorum. Pub/sub loss: because pub/sub is fire-and-forget, treat it as a latency optimization, and rely on the durable store plus client sync as the source of truth. Region failure: discuss it as an extension, not a core requirement. End-to-end encryption changes where search and server-side features can work, so mention it as a scoping question.

pressure_questions.q: A gateway holding 500,000 connections dies. Walk me through the next 60 seconds.
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Clients detect the closed connection and reconnect to other gateways with jittered backoff so the load spreads. Each client sends its last seen sequence number per conversation and the server replays missing messages from durable storage. Registry entries for the dead gateway expire by TTL, and messages sent in the gap are delivered on reconnect or by push notification. I cap per-gateway connections so survivors are not overloaded.

pressure_questions.q: How do you order messages across a user's two devices?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Order by the per-conversation sequence number assigned server-side, not device time. Each device syncs from its own last seen sequence, so both converge to the same order.

pressure_questions.q: A group with 100,000 members is extremely active. What breaks?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Per-member fan-out writes explode and its partition becomes hot. I'd not fan out per member for large groups. I store the message once, members pull by sequence number, push notifications are batched and rate limited, and I may split the partition by time bucket.

pressure_questions.q: Your pub/sub layer drops a message. Is the message lost?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: No. Pub/sub is only a fast path. The message is already persisted with a sequence number. The recipient notices a gap in sequence numbers or syncs on reconnect and fetches it from storage.

sessions.title: Storage engine internals: B-trees, LSM-trees, indexes, durability
sessions.goal: Explain why Cassandra writes fast and Postgres supports rich queries by describing how each stores data, and use that to predict behavior and failure modes.
sessions.warmup_note: 5 minutes. Answer out loud, then check.

warmup.q: Why shouldn't you use wall-clock timestamps to order chat messages?
warmup.a: Clocks drift and collide. Use a per-conversation sequence number assigned by the partition owner.

warmup.q: A 5-node Raft cluster tolerates how many failures?
