sections.heading: Why internals matter at a senior level
sections.body: Knowing how an engine stores data lets you predict behavior instead of memorizing database names. It explains why one store handles 100,000 writes per second and another handles complex joins, why deletes can hurt in some systems, why disk space needs headroom, and what slows down at the tail. In interviews it lets you justify 'wide-column store' with a reason beyond 'it scales'.

sections.heading: B-tree engines (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB)
sections.body: Data and indexes are organized in fixed-size pages (8 KB by default in Postgres, 16 KB in InnoDB). A B-tree has high fan-out, so hundreds of keys per page, which means even billions of rows need only 3 to 4 levels, and a lookup costs a few page reads (the top levels are usually cached in memory). Updates modify pages in place. To survive crashes, the engine first appends the change to a write-ahead log (WAL), which is sequential and fsynced, then modifies pages in memory (the buffer pool) and flushes them later. Writes involve random IO to scattered pages, page splits when a page fills, and every extra index means another tree to update. Postgres uses MVCC (multi-version concurrency control): an update writes a new row version and old versions linger until vacuum removes them, which is why long-running transactions and heavy update workloads cause bloat. Strengths: predictable read latency, efficient range scans, rich queries and transactions. Weaknesses: write throughput limited by random IO and single-primary architecture.

sections.heading: LSM-tree engines (Cassandra, RocksDB, HBase, ScyllaDB)
sections.body: A log-structured merge tree optimizes for writes. A write goes to a commit log (sequential append, for durability) and to an in-memory sorted structure called the memtable. When the memtable fills, it is flushed to disk as an immutable, sorted file called an SSTable. Over time there are many SSTables, so background compaction merges them, discarding overwritten and deleted data. Reads must check the memtable and potentially several SSTables, so engines use Bloom filters (a compact structure that says 'definitely not here' or 'maybe here') to skip files, plus sparse indexes and caches. Deletes write a tombstone marker that is only removed after compaction, so heavy deletion workloads can cause slow reads that scan many tombstones. The costs: write amplification from compaction (data is rewritten multiple times), read amplification, space amplification (you need free disk space for compaction to run, sometimes up to a large fraction of the data size with size-tiered compaction), and latency spikes when compaction competes with traffic. Compaction strategy is a dial: leveled compaction reduces read and space amplification but rewrites more; size-tiered favors write throughput.

sections.heading: Comparing them in one table (spoken)
sections.body: Write throughput: LSM is higher because writes are sequential. Read latency: B-tree is more predictable, LSM reads may touch multiple files. Range scans: both support them in key order; B-trees are very efficient. Updates in place: B-tree yes, LSM appends new versions. Space overhead: LSM needs compaction headroom, B-tree has page fragmentation and bloat. Transactions and joins: native in B-tree relational engines, limited in most LSM stores. Use the sentence: 'The workload is write-dominated and keyed, so I want an LSM-based store; if it were read-heavy with joins and transactions, I'd want a B-tree relational engine.'

sections.heading: Indexes beyond the basics
sections.body: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then the second, and so on, so column order must match query patterns: put equality-filtered columns first, then range or sort columns. A covering index includes every column a query reads, enabling index-only scans. A partial index covers only rows meeting a condition (for example only active rows), keeping it small. Selectivity matters: an index on a boolean column rarely helps. A B-tree cannot help with a leading wildcard such as LIKE '%abc', which needs a trigram or full-text index. Inverted indexes map terms to the documents containing them and power search engines. Geospatial indexes (geohash, quadtree, S2, H3) map two-dimensional locations to one-dimensional keys. Hash indexes support equality only. Every index slows writes and consumes storage, so a senior answer names which indexes the design needs and why, not 'index everything'.

sections.heading: Columnar storage and OLTP vs OLAP
sections.body: Row stores keep all columns of a row together, ideal for fetching or updating individual records (OLTP: online transaction processing). Column stores keep each column together, so analytic queries that scan a few columns over billions of rows read far less data, and similar values compress very well. Parquet, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Redshift, and Snowflake follow this model. They are poor at single-row updates. The standard architecture separates the two: the transactional database serves the application, and changes flow through CDC or batch ETL into a warehouse or lake for analytics, so heavy reports cannot degrade user-facing latency.

sections.heading: Durability, fsync, and failure
sections.body: A write is durable only after it reaches non-volatile storage, which means the fsync of the log, not just a write to the operating system's page cache. Some systems trade durability for speed by batching fsyncs, which risks losing the last moments of writes on a crash. Replication adds durability across machines; synchronous replication to another zone survives losing a node, and backups with point-in-time recovery (base backup plus the log) survive operator error, which replication does not protect against, because a bad delete replicates instantly. Checksums detect silent corruption. Disks and entire zones fail, so replication across zones is the baseline for important data.

sections.heading: Storage capacity math with real overhead
sections.body: Raw logical data is only the starting point. Multiply by replication factor (3), add index and metadata overhead (often 1.3x to 2x for relational data), and add headroom for compaction or vacuum and growth (keep disks well under full, often 50 to 70 percent used). Example: 6 TB logical x 3 replicas x 1.5 overhead is 27 TB, and at 60 percent target disk usage you provision about 45 TB. Saying this shows you understand that provisioned capacity is much larger than the data size in your first estimate.

key_terms.definition: Write-ahead log. Changes are appended sequentially before being applied, for crash recovery.
Multi-version concurrency control. Updates create new row versions so readers do not block writers.
Log-structured merge tree. Buffers writes in memory, flushes sorted immutable files, compacts in the background.
In-memory sorted write buffer and the immutable sorted file it flushes to.
Background merging of SSTables to discard stale data and bound read cost.
Bytes physically written per byte of user data.
Probabilistic structure with no false negatives and some false positives, used to skip files.
A delete marker retained until compaction.
An index that contains every column needed by a query.
Transactional single-row workloads versus analytic scans over many rows.
Point-in-time recovery using a base backup plus the log.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why are Cassandra writes so fast?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: A write is an append to a commit log plus an insert into an in-memory structure, both sequential and cheap. There is no in-place update and no random disk seek on the write path. The cost is deferred to background compaction and to reads, which may check several files, mitigated by Bloom filters.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why can heavy deletes cause problems in an LSM store?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Deletes write tombstones, and the data stays until compaction removes both. Reads that scan a range must skip over many tombstones, which slows queries. The design fix is to avoid delete-heavy patterns, use TTLs with time-bucketed partitions so whole partitions expire, and tune compaction.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Replication protects my data, so why do I need backups?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Replication copies mistakes instantly: a bad migration or accidental delete is applied to every replica. Backups with point-in-time recovery let me restore to before the mistake. I'd also test restores regularly, because an untested backup is a guess.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How would you size disk for 6 TB of logical data?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Multiply by 3 for replication, by about 1.5 for indexes and overhead, giving about 27 TB, then provision for 60 percent utilization to leave compaction and growth headroom, so about 45 TB across the cluster.

say_it_out_loud: This is write-dominated and keyed, so I want an LSM-based store: writes are sequential appends, and I accept read amplification mitigated by Bloom filters.
I'd keep this relational data in Postgres, because I need joins and transactions and the write rate fits a single primary.
Replication is not a backup, so I'd add point-in-time recovery and test restores.
Provisioned storage is six terabytes times three replicas times one-and-a-half overhead, then headroom for compaction.

drill.q: Why does Postgres need VACUUM?
drill.a: MVCC leaves old row versions behind after updates and deletes. Vacuum reclaims them.

drill.q: Composite index (status, created_at). Query: status = 'open' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Efficient?
drill.a: Yes. Equality on status then sorted range on created_at, served directly by the index.

drill.q: What does a Bloom filter guarantee?
drill.a: No false negatives: 'not present' is certain. Possible false positives: 'maybe present'.

drill.q: 10 TB logical, RF 3, 1.5x overhead, 60% target utilization. Provision?
drill.a: 10 x 3 x 1.5 = 45 TB, divided by 0.6 is 75 TB.

drill.q: Why separate analytics from the transactional database?
drill.a: Large scans compete for IO and cache with user-facing queries, and columnar warehouses are far better at analytics. Feed it via CDC or batch.

drill.q: What is the difference between a WAL and a backup?
drill.a: The WAL gives crash recovery of recent changes. A backup is a separate copy that lets you restore after loss or operator error. Combined, they enable point-in-time recovery.

sessions.goal: Reason about concurrency bugs (lost update, write skew), keep transactions local, and use sagas and idempotency when they cannot be. This sets up the payment capstone.

warmup.q: Why can't you rely on replication as a backup?
warmup.a: It replicates mistakes instantly. You need backups with point-in-time recovery.

warmup.q: An LSM store has heavy deletes and slow reads. Likely cause?
warmup.a: Tombstones that must be scanned until compaction removes them.

sections.heading: Isolation levels and the bugs they allow
sections.body: Transactions give atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (constraints hold), isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), and durability. Isolation comes in levels. Read committed: you never read uncommitted data, but a repeated read can return different values (non-repeatable read). It is the default in Postgres. Repeatable read / snapshot isolation: a transaction sees a consistent snapshot as of its start; it is the default in MySQL InnoDB and what Postgres provides at its repeatable read level. Serializable: the outcome equals some serial order of transactions, which prevents the remaining anomalies but costs throughput and may abort transactions with serialization errors that you must retry. Anomalies to name: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read (new rows appear matching a query), lost update (two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other), and write skew (two transactions read overlapping data, each writes a different row, and together they violate an invariant). Classic write skew: two on-call doctors both check that at least two doctors are on call and both go off call, leaving none.

sections.heading: Fixing lost updates and write skew
sections.body: Lost update fixes: make the update atomic in the database (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100), use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to lock the row while you read and modify it, use optimistic concurrency with a version column (UPDATE ... WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7, then check how many rows changed and retry on zero), or use compare-and-set. Write skew fixes: serializable isolation, locking the rows that the decision depends on, or materializing the constraint into something lockable (a row representing the shift). Pessimistic locking suits high contention on the same rows, optimistic suits low contention and avoids holding locks, at the cost of retries. Deadlocks occur when transactions wait on each other in a cycle; databases detect them and abort one, so always lock rows in a consistent order and keep transactions short.

sections.heading: Keep transactions local by design
sections.body: A transaction across multiple partitions or services is expensive and fragile. The senior move is to choose the shard key so a business operation touches one partition. Put a user's cart, orders, and balances under the same key if they are updated together. Place the entities of a booking in one partition. When that is impossible, you accept either a distributed transaction or a saga. Say it directly: 'I'll shard by account ID so a transfer within an account's partition is a local transaction, and cross-account transfers go through a saga with a ledger.'

sections.heading: Two-phase commit and why to avoid it across services
sections.body: Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks all participants to prepare (they durably promise they can commit and hold locks), and if all agree, tells them to commit. Problems: it blocks if the coordinator crashes after prepare, because participants hold locks and must wait; it has high latency (multiple round trips and fsyncs); and it reduces availability since all participants must be up. Databases use it internally (including distributed SQL systems that pair it with consensus, such as Spanner), and the XA standard exists for cross-database use. Across independent microservices and third-party APIs it is usually the wrong tool because you cannot make an external payment provider participate.

sections.heading: Sagas
sections.body: A saga breaks a business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it if a later step fails. Example order flow: reserve inventory, charge payment, create shipment. If shipment fails, refund the payment and release inventory. Orchestration: a central coordinator (a workflow engine such as Temporal, or a state machine in your service) tells each participant what to do and tracks state, which is easier to reason about and monitor. Choreography: services react to each other's events, which avoids a central point but makes the flow hard to follow. Design rules: every step and every compensation must be idempotent and retryable; persist the saga state so it survives crashes; order steps so that irreversible actions (sending an email, shipping goods) come last; and remember sagas lack isolation, so other readers can see intermediate states, which you manage with explicit pending statuses and semantic locks (an item marked reserved). Combine with the transactional outbox so each step's database change and its event are atomic.

sections.heading: Payments: the model to carry into the capstone
sections.body: Money systems favor correctness over throughput, and their volume is often modest, so the right store is frequently a relational database. Idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key with each payment request; the server stores the key with the request fingerprint and the result in a table with a unique constraint, and a retry with the same key returns the stored result without charging again. State machine: a payment moves through explicit states (created, authorized, captured, settled, failed, refunded) and only legal transitions are allowed, enforced with conditional updates. Ledger: record money movement as an append-only, double-entry ledger where every transfer writes a debit and a credit that sum to zero, and balances are derived or maintained as cached aggregates. Never update history, add corrections. Reconciliation: because external providers can fail ambiguously (a timeout does not tell you whether the charge happened), you periodically compare your records with the provider's settlement reports and resolve differences. Webhooks from the provider report asynchronous outcomes, and you verify their signatures and handle duplicates and out-of-order delivery. Never store raw card numbers; use tokenization through the provider to limit compliance scope.

sections.heading: Unique constraints, inventory, and reservations
sections.body: Anything that must be unique or limited (usernames, seats, stock) needs an atomic check-and-set in one place, not a read followed by a write in application code. Options: a unique index so the second insert fails; a conditional update with a row count check; a single-writer design where one process owns each resource; or a reservation with expiry (a hold on the seat for 10 minutes, converted to a booking after payment, and released by a background sweeper or TTL). Reservations separate 'I want it' from 'I got it' and make abandoned checkouts safe.

key_terms.definition: How much concurrent transactions can observe each other's effects.
Two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other.
Concurrent transactions each pass a check then write different rows, together breaking an invariant.
Detect conflicts at write time with a version check and retry.
Locks selected rows until the transaction ends.
Two-phase commit. Coordinator prepares then commits across participants. Blocking and slow.
Sequence of local transactions with compensating actions.
A step that semantically undoes a previous step.

Comparing your records to an external system's to find and fix discrepancies.
A temporary claim on a resource that expires if not confirmed.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: A client times out calling your payment API and retries. How do you avoid double charging?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: The client sends an idempotency key on every attempt. Server-side I insert the key with a unique constraint before doing the work, and store the final response against it. A retry with the same key returns the stored response, or waits if the first attempt is still in progress. I pass the same key through to the payment provider so the provider also deduplicates.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: The payment provider times out and you don't know if the charge succeeded. What now?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Mark the payment as pending or unknown, never as failed. Query the provider by our idempotency key or reference to find the real status, retry the query with backoff, and rely on the provider's webhook and daily reconciliation to resolve it. Don't release the order or retry the charge blindly.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why not use 2PC across your order, payment, and inventory services?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: The payment provider can't participate, 2PC blocks if the coordinator fails, and it ties the availability of all services together. A saga with compensations and idempotent steps keeps each service independent, at the cost of intermediate states that I model explicitly.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How do you prevent overselling the last item?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Make the decrement atomic in the database: update stock set quantity = quantity - 1 where id = X and quantity > 0, and check that one row changed. For checkout I use a reservation with expiry so carts hold stock temporarily, and a sweeper returns expired holds.

say_it_out_loud: I'll shard by account ID so a business operation stays on one partition and I can use a local transaction.
Cross-service flows use a saga with idempotent steps and compensating actions, with the saga state persisted.
Every payment request carries an idempotency key stored under a unique constraint, so a retry returns the original result.
The ledger is append-only and double-entry, and we reconcile against the provider's settlement reports.

drill.q: Two transactions both read balance = 100 and each subtract 30 by writing 70. What anomaly and a fix?
drill.a: Lost update. Use an atomic UPDATE balance = balance - 30 WHERE balance >= 30, or SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a version check.

drill.q: Postgres default isolation level?
drill.a: Read committed.

drill.q: Order saga: reserve stock, charge card, ship. Shipping fails. What runs?
drill.a: Compensations in reverse: refund the charge, release the stock reservation. Both must be idempotent.

drill.q: Why put irreversible steps last in a saga?
drill.a: Compensating them may be impossible (a sent email, a shipped package), so do them only after the reversible steps succeed.

drill.q: Write the SQL pattern for optimistic concurrency.
drill.a: UPDATE t SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?; if rows affected = 0, someone else changed it, so re-read and retry.

drill.q: How should a payment record's state change be enforced?
drill.a: As a state machine with conditional updates, for example UPDATE ... SET status = 'captured' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'authorized'.

sessions.goal: Apply a failure toolkit to every box in a design, design a distributed rate limiter, and do availability and tail-latency math.

warmup.q: What is write skew? Give the classic example.
warmup.a: Two transactions each pass a check on overlapping data and write different rows, breaking an invariant, such as two on-call doctors both leaving.

warmup.q: Why store an idempotency key with a unique constraint?

sections.heading: How real failures behave
sections.body: Failures are partial and messy. Crash failures are the easy kind. Gray failures are worse: a service is slow, drops some requests, or is intermittently wrong while still passing health checks. Slowness is more dangerous than being down, because callers wait, threads and connections pile up, queues fill, and the slowness spreads upstream. Correlated failures take out many components at once: a bad deploy, an expired certificate, a shared dependency, a full zone. Metastable failures are self-sustaining: a brief overload triggers retries, retries add load, and the system stays down even after the original trigger is gone. A senior engineer designs for these specifically: bounded waits, bounded retries, load shedding, and the ability to recover under load.

sections.heading: The resilience toolkit
sections.body: Timeouts: every remote call has one, chosen from the dependency's observed p99 plus a margin, and a deadline should propagate down the call chain so downstream work stops when the caller has given up. Retries: only for idempotent operations and transient errors, with exponential backoff and jitter, a cap on attempts, and a retry budget (for example retries limited to 10 percent of traffic). Retry amplification is a trap: if each of 3 layers retries 3 times, one failure at the bottom can generate 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls. Retry at one layer only. Circuit breaker: after a threshold of failures the breaker opens and calls fail fast for a cooldown, then half-open lets a few probes through before closing. Bulkheads: separate thread pools, connection pools, or instances per dependency or tenant so one bad dependency cannot consume all resources. Load shedding: when saturated, reject low-priority requests early (503) so high-priority ones still succeed. Graceful degradation: serve cached or partial results, hide a non-essential feature, or fall back to defaults. Hedged requests: send a duplicate request to another replica after a delay near p95 to cut tail latency, for idempotent reads only. Health checks and automatic failover, redundancy across zones, and DLQs complete the list.

sections.heading: Rate limiting: algorithms
sections.body: Purpose: protect services from overload and abuse, enforce fair use and quotas. Token bucket: a bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at R per second; each request takes a token, so bursts up to B are allowed and the long-run rate is R. It is the most common answer. Leaky bucket: requests enter a queue and drain at a fixed rate, smoothing traffic. Fixed window counter: count requests in each fixed interval; trivial, but a burst around a boundary can pass twice the limit. Sliding window log: store each request timestamp and count those within the last interval; exact but memory-heavy. Sliding window counter: weight the previous window's count by overlap with the current window, a cheap approximation. Choose token bucket when bursts are acceptable, and a sliding window when you need a strict cap.

sections.heading: Rate limiting: distributed design
sections.body: Where: at the edge or API gateway for global per-client limits, and inside services to protect specific dependencies. Key: per user ID, API key, IP, or tenant, sometimes several at once. State: shared counters in Redis. A fixed window is INCR plus EXPIRE. A token bucket needs an atomic read-compute-write, done in a Lua script so two servers cannot interleave. The trade-offs: an extra network hop per request (a few hundred microseconds to a millisecond), the limiter itself becoming a dependency, and hot keys for very large clients. Alternatives: each server enforces an approximate local limit (limit divided by number of servers) and periodically syncs, trading accuracy for no per-request hop. Failure behavior: decide fail-open (allow traffic if the limiter is down, protecting availability) or fail-closed (block, protecting the backend), and state the reason; fail-open is the usual choice for public APIs. Responses: HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, plus headers showing remaining quota. Distinguish rate limiting (policy per client) from load shedding (protecting the service regardless of client) and quotas (long-period allowances like monthly API calls).

sections.heading: Availability math
sections.body: Availability is the fraction of time the service works. 99.9 percent allows about 8.8 hours of downtime per year (about 43 minutes per month). 99.99 percent allows about 53 minutes per year. 99.999 percent allows about 5 minutes per year. Components in series multiply: three services each at 99.9 percent give 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999, about 99.7 percent, so every hard dependency lowers your ceiling. Redundant components in parallel improve availability: two independent replicas each at 99 percent give 1 - (0.01 x 0.01) = 99.99 percent, but only if failures are truly independent, which shared deploys, shared zones, and shared dependencies often violate. This is why you remove hard dependencies from the critical path, make them optional with fallbacks, or cache their results.

sections.heading: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, and tail latency
sections.body: An SLI is a measured indicator (successful request ratio, p99 latency). An SLO is the internal target for it (99.9 percent of requests succeed, p99 under 300 ms). An SLA is the contractual promise with consequences, usually looser than the SLO. The error budget is 1 minus the SLO: at 99.9 percent you may fail 0.1 percent of requests, and when the budget is spent you slow feature releases and invest in reliability. Use percentiles, not averages: the average hides the slow requests that users feel. Fan-out amplifies tail latency: if a request must call 100 backends and each has a p99 of 1 second, the chance that at least one is slow is 1 - 0.99^100, about 63 percent, so the user-visible latency is dominated by the tail. Mitigations include hedged requests, reducing fan-out, timeouts with partial results, and caching.

sections.heading: Safe deployments and recovery objectives
sections.body: Most outages follow changes. Deploy gradually: canary (a small slice of traffic first, with automatic rollback on error-rate or latency regressions), rolling updates, or blue/green (switch traffic between two full environments). Use feature flags to decouple deploy from release and to turn things off quickly. Make schema changes backward compatible with expand and contract: add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old column later. Define RPO (recovery point objective: how much data you can lose, measured in time) and RTO (recovery time objective: how long you can be down). They drive your replication mode, backup frequency, and whether you need a warm standby. Practice recovery: restore from backup, fail over, and run game days, because a plan that has never been exercised is a guess.

key_terms.definition: A component is degraded (slow or partly wrong) but not fully down.
Overload that sustains itself, typically through retries, even after the trigger ends.
Fails calls fast after repeated errors, then probes to recover.
Resource isolation so one failing part cannot exhaust shared resources.
Rejecting some requests under overload to keep the system healthy.
Duplicate request sent after a delay to reduce tail latency.

Measurement, internal target, contractual promise.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Design a distributed rate limiter for 1 million requests per second.
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: I'd enforce limits at the edge with a token bucket per API key. Counters live in a sharded Redis cluster keyed by the client, updated by a Lua script so the refill-and-take step is atomic. To avoid a Redis hop on every request at this volume, each gateway keeps a local token allotment pulled in batches from Redis, accepting small over-admission. If Redis is unreachable the limiter fails open with a conservative local cap, because blocking all traffic is worse. Rejections return 429 with Retry-After, and I'd monitor rejection rates per client.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: A downstream dependency becomes slow, not dead. What happens to your service?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Threads and connections wait, pools fill, latency rises, and the slowness cascades upstream. I prevent it with timeouts shorter than the caller's deadline, a bulkhead so this dependency has its own bounded pool, a circuit breaker that fails fast, and a fallback or degraded response. I'd alert on p99 and pool saturation, not just error rate.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Your service depends on 4 services each at 99.9 percent. What availability can you promise?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: If all four are hard dependencies in series, about 99.6 percent (0.999^4). To promise more, I'd make some dependencies optional with fallbacks or cached results, so they're not on the critical path.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How do you deploy a change that renames a database column without downtime?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Expand and contract. Add the new column, deploy code that writes both and reads the old, backfill existing rows, switch reads to the new column, stop writing the old one, and drop it in a later release. Each step is backward compatible and can be rolled back.

say_it_out_loud: Every remote call gets a timeout, retries happen at one layer with backoff and jitter, and a circuit breaker protects us from a slow dependency.
I'll rate limit with a token bucket per API key, with atomic updates in Redis, returning 429 with Retry-After, and failing open if the limiter is down.
Three hard dependencies at three nines give me about two-and-a-half nines, so I'm moving this one off the critical path.
I'd track p99 latency and error budget burn rather than averages.

drill.q: 3 layers each retry 3 times. Worst-case calls to the bottom service per user request?
drill.a: 27 (3 x 3 x 3). Retry at one layer only and use a retry budget.

drill.q: Request fans out to 50 backends, each p99 = 1 s. Probability at least one exceeds 1 s?
drill.a: 1 - 0.99^50, about 40 percent.

drill.q: How much downtime per year at 99.99 percent?
drill.a: About 53 minutes.

drill.q: Two independent replicas at 99% each. Combined availability?
drill.a: 99.99 percent, if failures are independent.

drill.q: Fixed-window rate limiter weakness?
drill.a: Bursts straddling a window boundary can pass up to double the limit.

drill.q: Difference between rate limiting and load shedding?
drill.a: Rate limiting enforces per-client policy. Load shedding protects the service by dropping some load when overloaded, regardless of client.

sections.heading: How to run this session
sections.body: Same routine: dictate, transcript into the note tab as 'Mock 3', AI scores, and your own three lines. Compare all six rubric categories to Mock 1 and Mock 2. Look for categories that are not moving and make them the focus of cycle 4.

sections.heading: What a strong answer contains
sections.body: Requirements: post, follow, view a reverse-chronological feed (ranking is out of scope but leave a hook for it), media, deletes and blocks. Numbers: about 23,000 feed reads per second average and 70,000 peak, about 2,300 posts per second, follow graph about 640 GB. Core design: a post service writes posts to a store partitioned by author; a follow graph store holds followers and followees; a fan-out service consumes post events from a queue and writes post IDs into followers' precomputed feeds, stored as capped sorted lists in a cache or fast store; the feed service reads the list, hydrates post details from a post cache and store, and returns a cursor-paginated page.

sections.heading: The fan-out decision and the hybrid
sections.body: Fan-out on write (push): when a user posts, insert the post ID into each follower's feed. Reads are cheap and fast. Writes multiply by follower count, so a celebrity post triggers tens of millions of writes, and work is wasted on inactive users. Fan-out on read (pull): at read time, fetch the latest posts from everyone the user follows and merge. Writes are cheap, reads are expensive and slow, especially for users following thousands of accounts. Hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrity accounts, and merge the celebrity posts into the precomputed feed at read time. Also skip precomputing feeds for inactive users and build theirs lazily on return. State the threshold (for example accounts above 100,000 followers are treated as celebrities) and why it exists.

sections.heading: Supporting problems senior candidates cover
sections.body: Feed storage: a per-user capped list of the latest few hundred post IDs (a Redis sorted list or similar), rebuilt from the post store and follow graph if lost. Cursor pagination uses (timestamp, post_id) so it is stable. Likes and comments: counters can be eventually consistent, using sharded counters or buffered increments aggregated asynchronously, with exact data kept in a separate store. Deletes and blocks: a deleted post must disappear from feeds, so hydration filters out missing or blocked posts, and a background job removes stale IDs. New follow: backfill the new followee's recent posts into the follower's feed. Media: object storage and CDN, processed asynchronously. Ranking: leave an extension point where candidate IDs from the feed store go to a ranking service, with feature data, but do not design the model. Failure: if fan-out workers lag, feeds are briefly stale, which is acceptable; if the feed cache is lost, rebuild lazily with throttling to protect the database.

pressure_questions.q: A user with 30 million followers posts. What happens in your system?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: That account is above the celebrity threshold, so I do not fan out on write. The post is stored and cached, and at read time each follower's feed service merges recent celebrity posts into their precomputed feed. This keeps write cost bounded at the price of a slightly more expensive read, which I mitigate by caching the celebrity post lists, which are shared by all followers.

pressure_questions.q: A user deletes a post that is already in 10 million feeds. What do you do?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: I don't try to delete from 10 million lists synchronously. I mark the post deleted, and the hydration step filters it out when feeds are rendered, so it vanishes immediately for users. A background job lazily cleans the stale IDs.

pressure_questions.q: Your feed cache cluster loses a shard. What happens?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Those users' feeds are rebuilt on demand from the post store and follow graph, so I throttle rebuilds and prioritize active users to avoid overloading the database. Replicas of cache shards reduce how often this happens.

pressure_questions.q: How do you store and update like counts for a viral post?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Increments are buffered or sharded across several counter rows or keys and aggregated asynchronously, because one hot row cannot take millions of updates. The displayed count is eventually consistent. Exact per-user like records are written separately for deduplication and the 'you liked this' state.

pressure_questions.q: How would ranking fit into this design?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: The feed store becomes the candidate generator. A ranking service takes candidate IDs plus user and post features, scores them, and returns an ordered page, with the chronological feed as a fallback if ranking times out.

sections.heading: Search
sections.body: A search engine is built on an inverted index: a map from each term to the list of documents containing it (a posting list). A query looks up each term and intersects or unions the lists, then ranks results, typically with BM25 (an improved TF-IDF that weighs term frequency and rarity). Text goes through analysis first: tokenization, lowercasing, stemming, stop words. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch split an index into shards, each a separate Lucene index with replicas. A query is sent to every shard (scatter), each returns its top results, and a coordinator merges (gather). New documents become searchable after a refresh, about one second by default, so search is near-real-time. The architectural rule: the search index is a derived view, never the source of truth. Keep the primary data in a database, and feed the index using CDC or an outbox so it can be rebuilt by replaying data. Reindexing without downtime uses a new index plus an alias switch. Typeahead (autocomplete) uses prefix structures such as tries or edge n-grams, caches the most popular prefixes, and tolerates staleness.

sections.heading: Geospatial
sections.body: Proximity queries ('drivers within 2 km') need an index that maps 2D locations to something sortable. Geohash encodes latitude and longitude into a string where shared prefixes mean nearby cells, which makes range queries on a standard key-value store possible. Its pitfall: points near a cell boundary can be close but have different prefixes, so you query the cell and its neighbors. A quadtree recursively splits space into four, splitting dense areas finer, which adapts to uneven density. S2 (Google) and H3 (Uber) divide the sphere into hierarchical cells; H3 uses hexagons, which have uniform neighbor distances. Databases offer geospatial indexes too (PostGIS). Write load matters: 1 million active drivers each sending a location every 4 seconds is 250,000 writes per second. You do not need durable history for every point, so keep current positions in memory (a Redis geo structure or a custom in-memory grid sharded by cell) and sample or batch to long-term storage for analytics. Shard by geographic cell, and watch for hot cells like airports and stadiums.

sections.heading: Media upload and processing pipelines
sections.body: Never stream large files through your app servers. The client asks the API for a presigned upload URL, then uploads directly to object storage (S3), using multipart upload for large files so parts can be retried and uploaded in parallel. An upload-complete event goes on a queue, and workers process the file asynchronously: virus scan, thumbnails, transcoding into multiple resolutions and formats, extracting metadata. Video streaming uses adaptive bitrate protocols (HLS or DASH): the video is cut into short segments in several qualities, and the player switches quality as bandwidth changes. Segments and playlists are served through a CDN. Store only metadata (owner, status, renditions, URLs) in a database. Deduplicate by content hash. Use lifecycle policies to move cold content to cheaper storage tiers. Know the cost drivers: storage volume and, above all, egress bandwidth.

sections.heading: Stream processing and time
sections.body: Batch processing computes over bounded datasets, stream processing over unbounded event streams (Flink, Spark Structured Streaming, Kafka Streams). Windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping, such as every minute), sliding (overlapping), and session windows (gaps of inactivity). Event time (when it happened) differs from processing time (when you saw it), and events arrive late and out of order, so streaming systems use watermarks to decide when a window is complete and allow late data to update results. The Lambda architecture runs batch and stream paths in parallel and merges them; Kappa uses only a replayable stream. Choose by whether you need exact historical recomputation and how much duplicated logic you can tolerate.

sections.heading: Approximate data structures
sections.body: When exact answers cost too much memory, use probabilistic structures. Bloom filter: set membership with no false negatives and tunable false positives; use it to skip disk lookups, avoid cache penetration, or check 'have I crawled this URL'. HyperLogLog: estimates the number of distinct elements in a tiny, fixed amount of memory (Redis uses about 12 KB with roughly 0.8 percent error) and supports merging; use it for unique visitors. Count-Min Sketch: estimates how often each item occurred, with overestimation error; combined with a small heap it finds top-K heavy hitters. A trending-topics design: stream events into windowed counts using a Count-Min Sketch per window, maintain a top-K heap, and publish results to a cache every few seconds. State that results are approximate and why that is acceptable.

sections.heading: Counters and aggregation at scale
sections.body: A single counter row updated by millions of clients becomes a hot spot because updates serialize on one row or key. Options: sharded counters (spread increments across N keys and sum on read), write buffering (accumulate in memory or in a stream and flush aggregates periodically), and approximate counts. The accuracy you need decides the approach: a payment total must be exact, a view count can lag and be slightly off.

sections.heading: Coordination services and service discovery
sections.body: ZooKeeper, etcd, and Consul provide a small, strongly consistent store used for leader election, distributed locks with fencing, configuration, and service discovery (which instances of a service are alive and where). They run as 3 or 5 node clusters using consensus. Applications register themselves, other services look them up (client-side discovery) or go through a load balancer or service mesh, which also adds retries, timeouts, mutual TLS, and observability. Use them for metadata and control, never as a general data store.

key_terms.definition: Map from term to the documents containing it.
A relevance scoring function weighing term frequency and rarity.
String encoding of a location where shared prefixes indicate proximity.
Hierarchical spatial cell systems for proximity queries.
Uploading a large file in independently retryable parts.
Video in segments at several qualities; player switches by bandwidth.
A stream-processing marker of how far event time has progressed.
Approximate distinct count in tiny fixed memory.
Approximate per-item frequency counts.
A counter split over several keys to avoid a hot row.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How do you find the nearest drivers to a rider?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Divide the map into cells with a hierarchical index such as H3 or geohash. Keep each driver's current cell and position in memory, sharded by cell. A query looks up the rider's cell and its neighbors, filters by distance, and ranks by ETA. Because updates are about 250,000 per second and only the latest position matters, I keep current state in an in-memory store and persist samples asynchronously.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Why not make Elasticsearch your primary database?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: It is optimized for search, offers weaker transactional guarantees, near-real-time visibility, and reindexing is common. I keep the source of truth in a database with proper durability and constraints, and rebuild the index from it via CDC or outbox events.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Count unique daily visitors for a very large site.
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Exact counting needs a set of every visitor ID, which is gigabytes per day. I'd use HyperLogLog, about 12 KB per counter with under 1 percent error, one per day or per page, and merge sketches for ranges. Exactness isn't needed for traffic analytics.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: A user uploads a 4 GB video. Walk me through it.
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: The client gets a presigned multipart upload URL and uploads parts directly to object storage in parallel, retrying failed parts. On completion an event enters a queue. Workers scan the file, transcode into HLS segments at multiple resolutions, generate thumbnails, and write metadata and status to the database. Playback goes through a CDN with adaptive bitrate. App servers never touch the bytes.

say_it_out_loud: The search index is a derived view fed by change data capture, so I can rebuild it, and the database remains the source of truth.
I'll index locations with H3 cells, keep current driver positions in memory sharded by cell, and query the rider's cell plus neighbors.
Uploads go straight to object storage with presigned multipart URLs, and processing is asynchronous.
For unique visitors I'd use HyperLogLog, accepting under one percent error for tiny memory.

drill.q: 1 million drivers, location update every 4 seconds. Writes per second?
drill.a: 250,000 per second.

drill.q: What problem do geohash neighbors solve?
drill.a: Nearby points across a cell boundary have different prefixes, so you query the neighboring cells too.

drill.q: Why does search need a refresh interval?
drill.a: New documents are only searchable after the index segment is refreshed, so search is near-real-time, about 1 second by default.

drill.q: Choose: exact vs approximate for monthly invoice totals, unique visitors, top trending hashtags.
drill.a: Invoice totals exact. Unique visitors approximate (HyperLogLog). Trending hashtags approximate (Count-Min Sketch plus heap).

drill.q: Why use presigned URLs for uploads?
drill.a: The client uploads straight to object storage, so large files do not consume app server bandwidth or connections.

drill.q: How do you avoid a hot counter row?
drill.a: Shard the counter across several keys and sum on read, or buffer increments and flush aggregates.

sessions.title: Production reality: multi-region, observability, security, cost, and evolution
sessions.goal: Add the senior wrap-up that most candidates skip: how it runs in multiple regions, how you know it's broken, how it's secured, what it costs, and how it grows from 1x to 10x.
sessions.warmup_note: 5 minutes. Answer out loud, then check.

warmup.q: What is the search index's relationship to the primary database?
warmup.a: It is a derived view fed by CDC or outbox, rebuildable. The database is the source of truth.

warmup.q: How many writes per second for 1M drivers updating every 4 seconds?
RPO vs RTO?
warmup.a: RPO is the acceptable data loss window. RTO is the acceptable downtime.

sections.heading: Multi-region: when and how
sections.body: Reasons: lower latency for distant users, surviving a whole-region outage, and data residency laws. Costs: complexity, cross-region latency (tens to hundreds of ms), replication lag, higher spend. Patterns: single region across multiple zones (the default, survives zone failure); active-passive (a warm standby region receives replicated data and takes over on failure, with an RTO of minutes and an RPO equal to the replication lag); active-active (several regions serve traffic). Active-active needs a data story: partition ownership by home region (each user or conversation has one home region that accepts writes, others read replicas), multi-leader with conflict resolution, or a globally consistent database like Spanner at a latency cost. Route users with geo-DNS or anycast. A senior answer states: 'Start with multi-zone in one region. I'd add a second region only when latency or disaster recovery requirements demand it, and I'd home each user to one region to avoid write conflicts.' Also state that backups you have never restored are not backups, and that failover must be rehearsed.

sections.heading: Observability: how you know it's broken
sections.body: Three pillars. Metrics: numeric time series, cheap and good for alerting. Use RED for services (rate, errors, duration) and USE for resources (utilization, saturation, errors). Logs: structured (JSON), with a correlation or request ID propagated across services so you can follow one request. Traces: distributed tracing records the path and timing of a request across services, usually sampled, to find which hop is slow. Alert on symptoms users feel (SLO burn rate, elevated p99, error rate) rather than every cause, to avoid alert fatigue, and keep dashboards for diagnosis. Per-component signals to name in an interview: queue depth and consumer lag, cache hit ratio, replication lag, connection pool saturation, disk usage, p99 latency per endpoint, and DLQ depth. Closing a design with 'here is how I would know it is broken' is a strong senior signal, and it takes 30 seconds.

sections.heading: Security and privacy basics
sections.body: Authentication proves who you are (OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect for delegated login; passwords hashed with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2; multi-factor authentication). Sessions versus tokens: server-side sessions can be revoked instantly; JWTs are stateless and scale easily but are hard to revoke, so use short expiry plus refresh tokens. Authorization decides what you may do (role-based or attribute-based), and must be enforced in each service that owns the data, not just at the gateway. Encrypt in transit with TLS everywhere, including between internal services, and at rest with managed keys; keep secrets in a secrets manager, not in code. Minimize and classify personal data (PII), set retention periods, and support deletion requests, which interacts with immutable logs and backups. Prevent abuse with rate limiting, input validation, and parameterized queries. For multi-tenant systems, enforce tenant isolation in every query (row-level security or tenant-scoped keys) because a missing filter is a data leak. For URL-fetching features, guard against SSRF. For payments, use provider tokenization to keep raw card data out of your systems.

sections.heading: Cost as a design dimension
sections.body: The major cost levers: data egress (bandwidth leaving the cloud, so use CDNs and compress), storage volume and tiering (hot, warm, cold, with lifecycle rules), replication factor and over-provisioning, cross-zone and cross-region traffic (chatty services across zones add up), and compute (autoscale stateless tiers, use reserved or committed capacity for steady load). Do the math: object storage is on the order of two cents per GB per month for standard tiers (check current pricing), so 1 PB is 1,000,000 GB, roughly $23,000 per month before replication in the provider's own durability, and requests and egress are extra. Caches cut database size and cost, but cache memory is pricier per GB than disk. A senior answer picks the cheapest design that meets the stated requirements and calls out where cost would explode, such as storing every raw location ping forever or keeping all media in hot storage.

sections.heading: Evolution: 1x, 10x, 100x
sections.body: Do not design for 1000x on day one. Start simple: a stateless app tier, one relational database, a cache, and object storage. Identify the first bottleneck, which is usually the database. The usual order of moves: add indexes and fix queries, add a cache, add read replicas, move async work to queues, partition hot tables, and finally shard or move specific workloads to specialized stores. In an interview, present the design for stated scale, then say what breaks first at 10x and what you'd change. Data migration without downtime follows a standard recipe: dual write to old and new, backfill history, shadow read and compare, switch reads, stop writing the old, and retire it. The strangler pattern replaces a monolith piece by piece behind a routing layer. Backward-compatible schema changes with expand and contract keep every step reversible.

sections.heading: Build vs buy, and multi-tenancy
sections.body: Managed services (managed databases, queues, caches) reduce operational burden and are usually the right default unless cost, control, or compliance says otherwise, and you can say 'I'll assume managed services are allowed.' Self-hosting is justified when you have the team to run it and the scale to benefit. In multi-tenant systems, noisy neighbors are a risk: apply per-tenant quotas and rate limits, isolate heavy tenants on dedicated capacity, and consider whether tenants share tables, schemas, or databases depending on isolation and compliance needs.

key_terms.definition: Standby region versus multiple regions all serving traffic.
Rate-Errors-Duration for services. Utilization-Saturation-Errors for resources.
Following one request across services with timing for each hop.
An ID attached to a request and logged by every service for it.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How would you make this survive a full region outage?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: First clarify the RPO and RTO. For minutes of downtime and seconds of data loss I'd run active-passive: continuous async replication to a standby region, infrastructure pre-provisioned, DNS failover, and regular failover drills. Data written in the last replication-lag window may be lost, which I'd state. If the business needs near-zero RTO, I'd move to active-active with each user homed to one region to avoid write conflicts.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: What would you monitor and alert on for this system?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: User-facing SLIs: success rate and p99 latency per critical endpoint, alerting on error-budget burn rate. Component health: consumer lag, cache hit ratio, replication lag, connection pool saturation, disk headroom, DLQ depth. I'd page on symptoms and use dashboards and traces for diagnosis, and propagate a request ID through every service for debugging.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: How do you migrate 5 TB from one database to another with no downtime?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Dual write new changes to both, backfill historical data in the background with throttling, run shadow reads comparing results, fix discrepancies, switch reads to the new store, then stop writing to the old one after a bake period with a rollback plan. Each step is reversible.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: A JWT is stolen. What can you do?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: With pure stateless JWTs I can't revoke it before expiry, so I keep access tokens short-lived, around 15 minutes, with refresh tokens that I can revoke server-side, and maintain a denylist for emergencies. Sensitive actions also require re-authentication.

say_it_out_loud: I'd start with multi-zone in one region and add a second region only when latency or disaster recovery demands it.
Here's how I'd know it's broken: error budget burn on the redirect endpoint, consumer lag, cache hit ratio, and replication lag.
I'm assuming managed services are allowed, and I'm choosing the cheapest design that meets the requirements.
At ten times this scale, the first thing to break is the primary database, and I'd move hot tables to a partitioned store.

drill.a: About 30 seconds of data.

drill.q: RED metrics stand for?
drill.a: Rate, Errors, Duration.

drill.q: Estimate monthly storage cost: 500 TB at about $0.023 per GB-month.
drill.a: 500,000 GB x 0.023 is about $11,500 per month (check current pricing, excluding egress and requests).

drill.q: List the steps of a zero-downtime database migration in order.
drill.a: Dual write, backfill, shadow read and compare, switch reads, stop old writes, retire the old store.

drill.q: Why enforce authorization in each service and not just at the gateway?
drill.a: Internal paths bypass the gateway and a gateway bug or misrouting would expose data. The data owner must check.

drill.q: Name two ways to cut egress cost for a media app.
drill.a: Serve through a CDN with high hit ratio and use compression and adaptive bitrate.

sessions.title: Senior communication: structure, trade-offs, pushback, recovery, and your own stories
sessions.goal: Convert knowledge into delivery. Practice the opening, the decision statement, handling pushback, getting unstuck, and closing, then audit your remaining weak spots.
sessions.warmup_note: 5 minutes. Answer out loud, then check.

warmup.q: State the four parts of a decision statement.
warmup.a: Decision with a number, the trade-off you accept, the alternative you rejected, and what would make you revisit.

warmup.q: Rewrite: 'I guess we could scale horizontally if the company allows.'
warmup.a: 'This tier is stateless, so I scale it horizontally behind a load balancer.'

warmup.q: What are the recommended phases and times of the 45 minutes?
warmup.a: 5 requirements, 5 estimation, 6 to 7 API and data model, 13 high-level design, 12 deep dive, 3 wrap-up.

sections.heading: What senior sounds like
sections.body: A mid-level candidate lists components. A senior candidate drives: they clarify scope, state assumptions, quantify, justify each choice, name the cost of that choice, anticipate failure, and manage time. They also know what to skip. You are a new grad, so interviewers will not expect depth in every area, but they do calibrate on habits, and these habits are teachable: structure, numbers, trade-offs, ownership, and calm. Your baseline review already credited you with strong instincts. This session is about delivery.

sections.heading: The first 90 seconds (script it)
sections.body: Restate the problem in one sentence to confirm. Then ask scoping questions in a fixed order so you never forget one: who uses it and at what scale (users, DAU), core features (and what is explicitly out of scope), read versus write mix, consistency and latency expectations, and constraints (platform, compliance). Then declare assumptions as a numbered list and say 'I'll proceed with these, tell me if any are wrong.' Example: 'I'll assume 100 million daily users, a 100 to 1 read to write ratio, delivery within a second, 99.9 percent availability, and that managed cloud services are available.' This single move eliminates the deferral problem from your baseline.

sections.heading: The decision statement
sections.body: Every significant choice gets four beats: the decision with its numeric reason, the cost you accept, the alternative you rejected, and the trigger that would change your mind. Example: 'Writes are about 70,000 per second at peak, so I'm using a partitioned wide-column store keyed by conversation. I'm giving up joins and ad hoc queries. I considered sharded Postgres and passed because I'd carry the sharding complexity without using relational features. If we later need rich reporting, I'd stream the data to a warehouse.' Practice making this statement in about 20 seconds. If you only say the first beat, you sound like you are guessing.

sections.heading: Whiteboard technique
sections.body: Draw the happy path first, left to right: clients, edge, services, stores. Number the steps of one request so you can narrate it. Label every datastore with its partition key and every queue with its message key. Put QPS and size estimates next to components. Draw one thing at a time and talk while drawing so you never go silent. Leave space to zoom in for the deep dive. Do not draw every service in the company, only what the problem needs. Sketch the API and the main tables compactly before the diagram so the interviewer sees your data model early.

sections.heading: Handling pushback and unknowns
sections.body: When challenged, do not cave and do not dig in. Ask what constraint changed, restate the concern, and evaluate it: 'Good point. If reads are 10 times higher than I assumed, the cache becomes the bottleneck, so I'd shard it and add an in-process layer.' When you do not know something precisely, say so and reason: 'I don't remember the exact figure, but the order of magnitude is tens of thousands of operations per second per node, and I'd validate it with a load test.' When you realize you made a mistake, say it directly and fix it: 'That unit is wrong, it's 6 TB, not 6,000, which means capacity isn't the issue.' Calm self-correction reads as senior. Silent flailing does not.

sections.heading: When you are stuck
sections.body: Say what you know, simplify, then build up. 'Let me start with the single-server version and see where it breaks.' Ask a constraint question instead of asking for the answer: 'Is stale data acceptable here?' Use your toolkit as a prompt checklist: where is the bottleneck, what is the failure mode, what is the hot key, what does it cost. If time is running out, tell the interviewer your plan: 'I have about eight minutes left, so I'll cover failure handling and monitoring briefly rather than the second deep dive.'

sections.heading: Choosing the deep dive
sections.body: Pick the part that is hardest and most specific to this problem: key generation and caching for a URL shortener; ordering, delivery, and connection scale for chat; fan-out for feeds; idempotency, state machines, and the ledger for payments; spatial indexing and write rate for ride-sharing; fan-out reliability and provider limits for notifications. If the interviewer steers you elsewhere, follow, because they are showing you what they want to see.

sections.heading: Close strong, and use your own work
sections.body: Spend the last two minutes on a 60-second summary: requirements, the design in one breath, the two or three key trade-offs, the first thing that breaks at 10x, and how you would monitor it. Also prepare to connect concepts to your own projects. TALOS is real material: it dedupes duplicate sends by message ID (idempotency), keeps the rest timer on stored timestamps so it survives the page being suspended (state outside the process), runs scheduled jobs with retries and last-good snapshots when a source fails (graceful degradation), uses row-level security and soft deletes with an action log for undo (auditability and safe writes), and keeps secrets server-side. Your event pipelines and multi-agent backend work are also concrete examples of queues, retries, and failure handling. One real story about what broke and what you changed is worth more than a recited pattern.

sections.heading: Weak-spot audit
sections.body: Open your note tab and read the three mock reviews and your own three lines for each. Count which of the six rubric categories were lowest on average and which terms you missed more than once. Write a one-page list of the top 10 terms you still hesitate on and say each definition out loud in one sentence. That list is your final-week study sheet.

key_terms.definition: The 10 to 15 minute section where you go detailed on the hardest part of the design.
The main flow when nothing fails. Draw it first.
Features you explicitly agree not to design.
The condition that would change a decision.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: I think your choice of database is wrong. Convince me.
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Good challenge. Here's my reasoning: the write rate is 70,000 per second at peak and access is by key with no joins, so I optimized for write scale. I accept the cost of limited queries. If you see a requirement that needs relational queries or transactions, tell me and I'll reconsider, for example by keeping that slice in Postgres and the high-volume data in the key-value store.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: You have 10 minutes left. What do you cover?
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: I'll spend about five minutes on failure handling for the two riskiest components, two on monitoring and the first bottleneck at 10x, and one on a closing summary. I'll skip the second deep dive unless you'd rather I do that.

interviewer_follow_ups.q: Tell me about a system you built that failed and what you changed.
interviewer_follow_ups.strong_answer: Use a concrete example from your own projects: what broke, how you detected it, the root cause, the fix, and what guardrail you added so it can't recur. Keep it to ninety seconds.

say_it_out_loud: Let me restate the problem and ask a few scoping questions before I draw anything.
I'll proceed with these assumptions. Tell me if any of them are wrong.
The decision is X because of this number. The cost is Y. I rejected Z. I'd revisit if W.
I have about eight minutes left, so here's what I'll cover.

drill.q: Record yourself giving the 90-second opening for a ride-sharing prompt. Check: restated problem, scale question, features, read/write mix, consistency, constraints, assumptions list.
drill.a: Self-check against the list. All seven elements should appear in order.

drill.q: Rewrite weak statement: 'Maybe a queue would help here.'
drill.a: 'Sending the receipt email doesn't need to block the response, so I'll put it on a queue and process it asynchronously with idempotent workers.'

drill.q: Rewrite weak statement: 'We'll just use NoSQL because it scales.'
drill.a: 'At 70,000 writes per second with key-based access and no joins, I'm choosing a partitioned wide-column store. I'm giving up joins. If we needed transactions across entities I'd reconsider.'

drill.q: Rewrite weak statement: 'I'm not sure about the numbers.'
drill.a: 'I don't remember the exact figure, but the order of magnitude is X, and I'd validate it with a load test. Let me proceed with that assumption.'

drill.q: Say a 60-second closing summary for the chat design out loud.
drill.a: Self-check: requirements, design in one breath, two or three trade-offs, first bottleneck at 10x, how you'd monitor.

sessions.title: Mock 4 (Capstone): Design a payment system, then the final review
sessions.goal: Use everything: estimation, storage choice from the math (which here points to a relational database), idempotency, state machines, sagas, reconciliation, and failure handling. Then run the final review against your baseline.

warmup.q: 10 million payments per day. Average and peak (10x) payments per second?
warmup.a: About 115 per second average, about 1,150 at 10x peak.

warmup.q: Two ledger entries per payment at 1 KB each, 10M payments per day. Storage per day and per year?
warmup.a: 20 GB per day, about 7.3 TB per year.

warmup.q: A request to the provider times out. What state do you record?
warmup.a: Pending or unknown, never failed. Then query by idempotency key and reconcile.

sections.heading: Why this is the capstone
sections.body: This prompt flips the pattern from your baseline. The math here is gentle: about 115 payments per second on average and about 7 TB per year. A single relational database with replicas handles that comfortably, and the value of Postgres (transactions, constraints, joins) matters a great deal. Your baseline said you default to SQL even when the math points to NoSQL. This design tests the opposite skill: letting the math point to SQL, and spending your time on correctness. Say it explicitly: 'The volume is modest and correctness dominates, so I'm choosing a relational database and I'll spend the design effort on idempotency, state, and reconciliation.'

sections.heading: What a strong answer contains
sections.body: Requirements: merchants charge customers, support card payments through an external provider (the processor), refunds, webhooks, and a ledger; correctness and auditability over speed; no raw card data stored. Numbers: 115 per second average, 1,150 peak, about 7 TB per year of ledger data. Core design: an API gateway with auth and rate limiting, a payment service, a PostgreSQL primary with synchronous replication to a standby in another zone, and an async path through a queue for provider calls, webhooks, and notifications. Tables: payments (id, merchant_id, amount, currency, status, idempotency_key unique per merchant), ledger_entries (append-only, double-entry), and an outbox. The deep dives follow.

sections.heading: Deep dive options
sections.body: A) Idempotency and retries: unique constraint on (merchant_id, idempotency_key), store the request fingerprint and response, handle in-flight duplicates by waiting or returning a conflict, pass the key to the provider. B) The state machine: created, authorized, captured, settled, failed, refunded, with conditional updates for legal transitions, and what you do when a provider call times out (pending, then resolve by querying and webhooks). C) The ledger and reconciliation: append-only double-entry, balances derived with a cached aggregate, daily reconciliation against provider settlement files, and a process for discrepancies. D) Webhooks: verify the signature, respond quickly with 200, enqueue for processing, dedupe by event ID, tolerate out-of-order delivery by checking state versions. E) Scaling and sharding: shard by merchant ID if volume grows, keep each payment's data on one shard so transactions stay local, and handle a very large merchant as a hot key. F) Security and compliance: tokenization so card numbers never touch your systems, encryption, audit logs, least privilege, and PCI scope reduction.

sections.heading: Final review protocol
sections.body: After the mock, do these in order. 1) Paste the transcript and AI scores into the note tab as 'Mock 4'. 2) Export all System Design entries: your baseline review, Mocks 1 to 4, and your own three-line notes. 3) Paste the final review prompt from this file, plus all entries, into a new AI chat. 4) Save the result in the note tab as 'Final review'. 5) Make a small table in the note tab with your six category scores for baseline, Mock 1, 2, 3, and 4, and the final review, so the trend is visible at a glance. 6) Write your own conclusion: where you improved, what remains, and what you'd study next. Use the final review as one signal. Your own list of mistakes is more reliable than any single AI grade.

mock.prompt: Design a payment processing system for an online platform. Merchants charge customers' cards through an external payment provider. The system must be correct, auditable, and handle retries safely. Support payments, refunds, and asynchronous provider notifications. (Alternate prompt if you want a second try later: design a ride-sharing dispatch service.)

clock.what_to_do: Ask about payment methods, currencies, refunds, who holds card data, settlement timing, and audit needs. Declare: 10M payments per day, 10x peak, 99.99 percent availability for the charge API, no raw card data stored, external provider handles card networks.

About 115 per second average, about 1,150 at 10x peak. Ledger about 20 GB per day, about 7.3 TB per year. So-what: low throughput, high correctness, relational database is appropriate. Be explicit that the math chooses SQL here.

POST /payments with Idempotency-Key header, GET /payments/{id}, POST /payments/{id}/refunds, POST /webhooks/provider. Tables: payments, ledger_entries, idempotency_keys (or columns), outbox_events, webhook_events.

Gateway, payment service, Postgres primary with sync standby, queue and workers for provider calls and notifications, webhook receiver, reconciliation job, ledger. Trace a successful payment, then a timeout.
Choose two from A to F in the notes above. Idempotency plus the state machine plus timeout handling is the strongest pairing.
Monitoring (success rate, pending-payment age, reconciliation mismatches, webhook lag), what changes at 10x, and the final 60-second summary.

numbers_to_hit: About 115 payments per second average, about 1,150 at peak
About 7 TB per year of ledger data, so one relational cluster is fine
Explicitly state that the numbers justify Postgres here
must_say_terms: webhook (correct usage: provider to your server)

pressure_questions.q: The provider call times out. Did the customer get charged?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: I don't know, so I never mark it failed. The payment stays pending. I query the provider using our reference and idempotency key with backoff, and the provider's webhook and the daily reconciliation resolve it. The customer isn't charged again because any retry uses the same idempotency key at the provider.

pressure_questions.q: Two identical requests with the same idempotency key arrive at the same instant.
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Both try to insert the key row; the unique constraint lets exactly one succeed. The other either waits for the first to finish and returns the stored response, or returns a 409 indicating the request is in progress. Never both executing the charge.

pressure_questions.q: The webhook says a payment succeeded, but your database says it failed. What happens?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: The webhook is evidence of the provider's truth, so I treat the provider as the source of truth for money movement. I verify the signature, dedupe by event ID, check the transition is legal for the current state, update the state and ledger in one transaction, and flag the discrepancy for review. Reconciliation catches any that slip through.

pressure_questions.q: How do you prevent the ledger from drifting out of balance?
pressure_questions.strong_answer: Entries are append-only and written in one transaction as balanced debit-credit pairs, enforced by a check on the transaction total. Corrections are new entries, never edits. A periodic job verifies that the sum of all entries per account matches cached balances and that totals match the provider's settlement reports.

That is about 115,000 per second at peak, so the primary becomes the bottleneck. I'd shard by merchant ID so each payment's transaction stays on one shard, move reads to replicas, use queues to smooth bursts, and handle very large merchants as hot keys with dedicated capacity. The ledger could move to a partitioned store with strict per-account sequencing.

common_traps: Choosing NoSQL by reflex when the volume is modest
Marking a payment failed after a timeout
No idempotency key or checking it in application code instead of a unique constraint
Updating balances in place with no ledger
Using 2PC across the external provider
Treating a webhook as a WebSocket or missing signature verification
Storing raw card numbers
